speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE FROM BARTIBOG, NEW BRUNSWICK, TO NEWCASTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that the management of the Canadian National Railways have received from Heath Steele Mines Limited, a subsidiary of American Metal Company, a request for the construction of a branch line from Barti-bog, New Brunswick, to the company's mine located some 30 miles northwest of Newcastle. Bartibog is on the main line of the Canadian National between Newcastle and Bathurst. The proposed branch line would be approximately 22 miles in length.
The management have made an appraisal of the economics of the proposed branch line and have concluded that it can be operated on a profitable basis. Accordingly, the management have asked the government to seek legislative authority for the construction of the line. It is the intention of the government at the first convenient opportunity to recommend the necessary legislation to parliament.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like Bills Nos. 158 and 188 dealt with separately.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 158, for the relief of Lorinc Orvos Nagy-Mr. Henderson-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
On clause 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, I am a member of the committee which dealt with this bill and I believe that special consideration should be given to this particular bill which involves a petition for divorce by Mr. Nagy. In view of the representations made by some of us in the committee and in view of the evidence presented before the committee of the other place, I believe there is good reason for a close examination of the evidence dealing with this divorce bill.
The petitioner works as a pipefitter and the respondent is a dishwasher. I presume she is a rather poor person, particularly so after she left the home. In the past certain investigators have come before us and given evidence in divorce cases. One of the investigators in this case had been in the employ of Harry Maxim, and in the past some of the evidence given by Mr. Maxim and his employees before the committee has proved to be very doubtful indeed.
There is also doubt with respect to the establishment of adultery in this case, and I think it behooves us as members of the house to pay particular attention to the proceedings in this case. The respondent is of Hungarian descent and speaks little or no English. Apparently she was not given an interpreter before the Senate committee and much of the evidence is very confusing, if not entirely unintelligible. I think that is an additional reason why members of the committee and of the house have a real point of argument in urging that a better method be provided to deal with divorce cases. This case lends weight to the argument that it is not appropriate for a committee of the house or even of the other place to deal with such an important matter as breaking up homes

and to pass laws which have the effect of bringing about the separation of men and women.
I want to deal particularly with the evidence in this case but before I go into that may I say that there seems to be doubt as to the jurisdictional powers of the committee of this house and the committee of the other place. On page 14 of the evidence taken in the other place I find that the chairman of the committee, Senator Ross, is asking certain questions and he has this to say:
I probably went too far. If the petitioner has been guilty of misconduct, it is a discretionary matter for us to refuse the divorce. Perhaps I went too far in my statement. You may go ahead.
Here is one instance where the chairman of the committee of the other place indicates that it is a discretionary matter whether or not the divorce will be granted if it is proved that the petitioner has been guilty of misconduct. I am particularly interested in this case because after reading the evidence carefully I am convinced that if there is any establishment at all on circumstantial evidence, then I would say there has been established the likelihood that adultery was committed on the part of the petitioner. Then too there is the fact that according to the authority of the other place there is some talk that they may also refuse to admit divorce on the ground of cruelty. In this case I might say that cruelty has been established. I understand that the respondent has not entered application for a rehearing of the case but it is important that she put in an appearance and contested the case. The facts of the matter are these.
First there is established the fact that the petitioner granted a mortgage to the respondent of $7,000 and agreed to pay a monthly allowance of $100. Here again I think there is the element of collusion between the parties that could be expected. It does not seem reasonable to me that the husband would give a mortgage of $7,000 and agree to pay $100 a month to his wife if she was to remain in the home. But that is the argument put up by the counsel for the petitioner. Then it is established that this payment was made for a period of some 10 months. That is agreed by counsel also. In the evidence it is indicated that the parties were quarreling and could not get along. It seems to me that the evidence points to the fact that the months of fighting which took place prior to her leaving home was, of course, the reason for her leaving home. It appears to me that the fact that he agreed to pay her $100 a month would indicate that he was paying in order that she would agree to leave the home and

leave the child with the husband. When the petitioner was asked if he was aware of adultery having been committed, we find on page 10 of the evidence this question and answer:
Q. You know nothing about the adultery? II she did commit adultery with another man?
A. I don't know. I just heard.
Then another important thing is that when the respondent was asked whether or not she had committed adultery she categorically said she had not. Throughout the whole examination and cross-examination there is no place where the woman has admitted to committing adultery. Again, I should like to point out that it seems to me that in the other place, in order to establish adultery in some cases and to elicit information which would lead to that establishment, certain leading questions are asked. As an example, I would point out that at page 11 Senator Ross asked of the petitioner this question:
Q. Have you forgiven her for the adultery at all?
A. No. I sorry.
Q. Did I understand you to say earlier that you are now living with your wife?
A. No, she not living with me.
It seems that after a few minutes of cross-examination we have Senator Ross asking if he condones the adultery before it is established whatsoever in the evidence. I think it is indicative that here is a whole procedure which should properly be under court jurisdiction either by the exchequer court or some other court designated to take care of cases of this sort. When these witnesses and investigators come before us we have not the authority to swear them, and if there is any perjury we cannot charge them with perjury. These people, both witnesses and investigators, can come before us and give any kind of evidence in order to try to establish their case, but there is no legal responsibility upon them. We are, therefore, in a very difficult position in trying to determine whether or not we can accept the testimony and statements made.
Now, of course, in this case the husband admits that he beat his wife. She left the home, and I feel that he tried to get her to accept money to leave the home and leave the child with him. Then, finally, the husband got his lawyer to interview the investigators and they have tried to build up a charge of adultery against her. I am not too sure of the legal position of the parties after we have passed an act on the basis of adultery which will dissolve the marriage. I am not sure how this may affect the respondent and the husband in the future. It might prejudice the woman in respect to the child, and she indicates she would like to have the child.

I point out that the child, a girl of 14, was with the wife for some seven of the ten months during which the wife was absent from the home. The wife returned to the home and again the husband beat her and drove her from the home. I think the least we can say about the wife's conduct is that she has tried to some extent to resolve their difficulties and has indicated her desire to have the child. I feel that the evidence in this case is so conflicting that the least we could do would be to have a rehearing so that the committee might have the petitioner and the respondent, as well as all the witnesses, before it to determine whether or not the committee would believe their testimony.
At the moment I might say that I have gone through the evidence very carefully, as I believe the other members of this group have. When we were dealing with this particular bill in the committee we asked that it be reheard. I am today, Mr. Chairman, asking that this bill be held over and not passed at this time. As I said earlier, I believe the purpose of the payment was merely to enable the husband to get rid of his wife and have her leave the child with him. There is a great deal of conflicting evidence given by the two investigators. I do not want to deal with all of it, but there is one statement I should like to mention.
Here, Mr. Greenblatt is examining one of the investigators, who said:
The room, I think, is about six by twelve and there is one bed, and a bureau and cot and a table in the room.
On the next page, under cross-examination by Mr. Gazdik, the defence counsel, the investigator said:
Q. Well, you said there was a bed and a cot?
A. No, a couch, which is not a cot.
Apparently, it is quite important in giving this evidence to establish what kind of room it was and what furniture was in the room in order to try to establish whether or not there has been misconduct. The witnesses seem to be confused in testifying before the committee.
I think, Mr. Chairman, this is one case in which we should at least have a rehearing so that the members of the committee could decide for themselves whether or not a divorce should be granted. I do not think we can take the responsibility for what has been done in the other place. I think the members of the other place are doing as good a job as they know how to do. They are in much the same position as we are in the committee of which I am a member. Their jurisdiction is relatively narrow. They can swear these witnesses but they cannot charge

them with perjury. I believe they are limited to making the one decision as to whether or not a divorce should be granted. I feel, sir, that the time has come when these divorce cases should no longer be brought before this house. In this case I am certainly making the strongest protest I can. I think it has been established that the respondent has been cruelly treated and that the husband concocted the idea of getting rid of his wife by agreeing to pay her a certain amount of money if she left home. He then got an investigator, but even the investigator's testimony before the committee of the other place does not establish in fact, except by circumstantial evidence, that adultery had been committed. Later the respondent herself denied the adultery. Then, we have the committee of the other place passing this bill on the basis of circumstantial evidence. I feel that the circumstantial evidence in this case is not strong enough to warrant the passage of the bill.
I feel that the woman had to live somewhere. She probably had few friends. The mere fact she was living in another place, apart from her husband, and a place in which there was a man living does not, of itself, indicate misconduct. Then, the woman had to go into the tobacco fields after leaving home. She did wait for a while to get her daughter to come with her, and she had to wait until the husband gave her $100. All this indicates to me she was under coercion, and I think if we are going to continue to have a process under which these petitions can come before this parliament, then a proper procedure should be followed. The parties should have proper counsel and interpreters should be provided so the evidence given will be intelligible. If a rehearing of the case is necessary, money should be available so that the parties will get justice. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I hope the members of this committee will agree to allowing this measure to stand to enable the committee to have a rehearing of the whole case.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee wish me to put the yeas and nays?
Yes.

Before we discuss this further, I want to say that this is one of the cases that when it came before the committee in the other place they were fortunate enough to have counsel for the respondent to put the respondent's case before that committee and to properly handle the evidence. I might say further that the counsel was a very reputable counsel.
I wonder if the hon. member would speak a little louder? We cannot hear him down in this corner?

With respect to the comments made about the investigator, I realize the hon. member who has just spoken certainly believes in the principles of British justice. Under this system a person is innocent until proven guilty. Nothing has been brought forward in this case to prove that the petitioner has not given truthful evidence.
The hon. member spoke about the variation which existed between the evidence given by the two investigators. It is frequently better to have evidence which does not stand too pat, when each witness gives his evidence and tells the story as he sees it, and thereby puts the true facts as he understands them. Nothing in the evidence suggests that these investigators did anything but the best job possible.
In this case the respondent was represented by counsel and that party could be presumed to have the proper legal advice to present the best evidence for her at the hearing. If they were not satisfied with the conduct of the hearing in the other place, counsel for the respondent could have so advised the clerk of the other place and they could have appealed it. Such was not the case. I cannot recall that any correspondence was produced or passed on to the chairman of the committee to the effect that the respondent in this case was not satisfied with the conduct of her defence. If she sincerely felt she would have a good defence I would think she would have pursued the matter further. She or her counsel could have appeared before the committee. Simply because there was some objection in another case we cannot say that it would appear there is an objection in this matter. No objection was made to the evidence given by the investigator and all the other facts were taken into consideration by the committee.
With respect to property rights I might say that the committee of the other place has no jurisdiction to deal with them. My hon. friend mentioned the sum of $7,000, which was by the way of a mortgage. At that time the petitioner was questioned by counsel for the respondent as recorded at page 14 of the proceedings:
Q. When is before?
A. In 1954, no, 1953, when we are fighting. We are fighting and I don't want to lose my daughter, my Esther. I don't want to lose her and she tell me if I offer her $7,000 she is not going to break the family life up.
There followed some discussion about making monthly payments of $100. As I recall

the evidence, the wife left voluntarily after a payment or two had been made. As the result of her leaving, the petitioner a short time after brought his petition to the committee of the other place and so carried it through.
I simply wished to make these remarks and to recall what happened according to the evidence. I thought it important to point out the courses of action which were opened to the respondent, who was represented by counsel, which courses were not taken either by the respondent or by counsel acting on her behalf. The facts as proved in the case must speak for themselves. Those who pass these bills must take the responsibility for them.

Mr. Chairman, as I have indicated on second reading, this bill comes before us from the province of Newfoundland. I realize that is a long way from Ottawa; however, I have yet to hear it said that the degree of justice that is handed out to Canadian citizens is dependent upon their nearness to the capital city, Ottawa. I believe that the citizen living on a far-flung island in the Pacific, or in the Artie ocean or on the island of Newfoundland, is subject to equal treatment, provided he is living in Canadian territory, when he appears before this House of Commons.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
This case is rather unique. It has come before what some people like to think of as the highest court in the land. Neither the petitioner nor the respondent is asked to appear and I cannot undertake to support this procedure in any way, shape or form. At home when you are accused of violating a minor traffic offence such as over-parking, if there is a parking meter or a time limit on parking you may mail in your fine and by so doing you are pleading guilty. However, if the charge is a little more serious a different condition may exist. In my home city if you are accused of having gone through an intersection wrongly you cannot even be represented by counsel without making a personal appearance, and you must plead guilty or not guilty. If you plead or are found guilty you must pay the fine. For a mere matter of crossing an intersection wrongly you must appear in person, yet when we are considering legislation that will break up what should be one of the holiest and most sanctified things in human society this parliament is willing to stand idly by and let the thing slide through in a manner which is as slipshod as could be found in any court case that I have ever heard of, and yet we have the temerity to call this the highest court of the land.
Getting down to the details of this particular case, we have affidavits to show that the petitioner has complied with all the rules of the other place and that notice has been served on the respondent. I assume that there is an affidavit to the effect that she has received this notice. However, in Canadian life we often hear of people signing affidavits which set out something that is not the fact. If this is allowed to continue you or I may find ourselves being divorced by the parliament of Canada without our being aware of what is taking place. That is possible if this procedure is allowed to get firmly rooted. The other day while we were in committee we passed some 111 of these bills in a matter of 18 seconds and I can well imagine the name of one of us being on that list without our being aware that we were being divorced. Some hon. member who did not belong to the same political movement might be willing to sign an affidavit to the effect that he had personally served us with the necessary legal documents some months ago.
I submit that it is hardly good enough. In most cases we are not satisfied with having just one witness, as we feel there should be corroborating evidence by two, three or sometimes four witnesses who could swear as to the adultery or whatever incident the divorce was being based on. In this case we have one single individual, a garage mechanic who

was in Newfoundland at the time. He appeared before the committee of the other place and testified that he had known the petitioner, having met him on a number of occasions. The petitioner was a salesman and this witness having heard that he was in town staying at one of the hotels decided to call on him around seven o'clock in the evening. He found that his friend was registered in a certain room, he went up to the room, opened the door and saw the man in bed with a woman. He immediately excused himself, went out and closed the door behind him. That is the only evidence on which this divorce is based and I do not think it is good enough.
In the committee it was said that we could not call in all these people, and the question was asked: Who is going to pay the expenses? Has this parliament reached such a low level that when a committee wants to hear witnesses we are to be floored by the question: Where is the money to come from? We have all kinds of money for other purposes, as this parliament votes some $5,000 million, but when a committee wants to hear witnesses it should have the right to hear, we are met with the question: Where is the money to come from? That argument was used in the committee stage and I believe it had some weight with members of the committee. After all, if we are not able to guarantee these people their expenses perhaps we ought not to call them here. I realize that calling people from Newfoundland would cost a considerable amount of money, but that money ought to be provided.
I submit that the evidence in this case is very slight. There is no corroboration whatsoever. The petitioner does not have any personal knowledge of the adultery. But this divorce is before parliament and we must take that for granted, but the fact is that I have seen enough affidavits which did not mean anything. I am unwilling to let this bill go by without making the most serious objection and I intend to call for the yeas and nays.

speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 158, for the relief of Lorinc Orvos Nagy.

Mr. Speaker, I had hoped that it would be unnecessary to make any remarks at this stage, but in view of the fact that there were only some 60 hon. members in the chamber when we were in committee I am sure that many hon. members would like to register their vote in connection with this particular bill. The hon. member for Moose Mountain has reviewed the case, I think, and so I do not plan on going over it in detail. I simply say that here is a petition which comes to us recommended by the other place, in which the petitioner appears to have been willing to give a mortgage of some $7,000, to be paid on an instalment basis at $100 a month commencing in about three months' time, on condition that his wife left the domicile. She appears to have left. Apparently, after having made ten payments, on advice of counsel, the petitioner found out that this was not necessary. As recorded on page 14 of the evidence, the counsel says:

Private Bills
And, he stopped making the payments in the first place according to my advice because the wife cannot be given anything in the form of a mortgage under the laws of Quebec.
But it seemed to be established that the husband was willing to pay $7,000 to get his wife out of sight so that another woman might take her place in the home. As recorded on page 11 of the evidence, the question was asked regarding this other woman who took over the wife's place:
Q. You refer to a housekeeper. Is it a male or female housekeeper?
A. Well, it is female housekeeper.
Q. You describe her as a housekeeper?
A. She work for me with money. I pay her $50 a month.
I should explain that these people are Hungarian. They are able to understand English, but they have some difficulty with the language, and this is how it appears in the evidence:
Q. Have you any receipts for that?
A. Me not need any receipt for that.
Q. Then you cannot prove or establish that you did pay any money at all?
A. Well, sure. Well, she was prove it. I not call anybody when I pay her.
Q. No. You had no witnesses and no evidence that you pay her?
A. I told the truth.
Further on, he was asked some questions about the living quarters. He said:
I have three rooms and a kitchen-or four rooms and kitchen.
After a little more thought he was sure there were four rooms and a kitchen. The owner of this domicile, who was apparently prepared to bear a mortgage for $7,000 to get rid of his wife, appears according to his evidence to sleep on a couch in the dining room through which his housekeeper must pass in going to the room where she sleeps and where he keeps his clothing. There is no doubt about the fact that he is living in these private quarters with someone who claims to be his housekeeper, although he has no evidence that he had paid an amount. Then counsel for the wife says:
I don't want to elaborate on this point but the fact remains there is a woman living in the same flat for some reason and I have no proof that the two have committed adultery . . .
Further on he says:
. . . that becomes very important because since the woman is in the place Mr. Nagy has not re-offered his wife to return to the place, and I have before that proof that an offer was made by Mr. Nagy for her to return and Mrs. Nagy wanted to return to the place, and still wants to return to the place-

Then Senator Ross, chairman of the committee, said:
I do not think the inquiries you have been following are very material because the petitioner is not on trial here. The question is not whether or not he committed adultery. The question is whether or not the respondent committed adultery.
Later on the chairman, Senator Ross, said:
I probably went too far. If the petitioner has been guilty of misconduct, it is a discretionary matter for us to refuse the divorce.
Counsellor for the petitioner had previously said:
But you should have somebody to testify here. She is living with him just the same as the roomers are living in the house.
He was asked:
You have no evidence at all on that?
The lawyer said:
No. I have no evidence.
This woman has considered the costs involved in bringing witnesses to Ottawa to appear on her behalf. It would seem to me, since there is a 14 year old1 child who apparently prefers to be with the mother, and since the mother is anxious to make a go of it and is forced to wash dishes at something around $20 a week to support herself and the child, we have a responsibility to decide whether or not an injustice will be done to one or the other. I do not think there is much likelihood of the two parties being reconciled, but I think this parliament has a responsibility to do something on behalf of this 14 year old girl, who does deserve some consideration.
So I would like to appeal to my friends from Quebec who are familiar with this case. It is significant that a member of parliament from the area has not risen to put in a good word for the petitioner. I want to thank the members of the Progressive Conservative party who have reviewed the evidence and who feel that they cannot put their vote of approval on the granting of this particular divorce when the evidence is as it was set out in the document that has come to us from the other place. Therefore, I wish to have the bells rung so that all members will have a chance to decide whether or not this woman should be given the protection of this chamber.

There are several comments I should like to make on this particular bill. In reading the evidence submitted to us from the committee of the other place, we are struck by the similarity between the various cases before the committee. This case is a little different in that there is perhaps no other instance where circumstantial evidence played such a great part.

As my colleagues have pointed out, there is no absolute proof of wrong-doing in this particular case. The petitioner is being granted a divorce purely on circumstantial evidence. The woman has attested to the case and has put forward her side of the story and has flatly denied any wrong-doing. Yet, on the basis of purely circumstantial evidence, the committee of the other place has seen fit to grant this divorce. It seems to me that a great deal of the argument, as revealed in the evidence, had to do with the question of the petitioner paying his wife $100 a month, and there were two points of view put forward. The counsel for the petitioner tried to make a case that the husband was paying the wife money to stay at home. Of course, the wife's counsel pointed out, quite rightly, that the money had been paid to the wife on the understanding that she leave the home. It seems to me it is rather unusual that the man in this case would agree to pay money under these circumstances. One will note in the evidence presented before the committee that the wife left the domicile on January 5, 1954. As recorded on page 16 of the evidence, Senator Barbour asked this question:
Q. I would like to know how many monthly payments he made, how many months he paid this $100 after his wife left?
A. Ten months.
Q. After she left you?
A. Yes. After she send me two months' notice, and, in March, 1954, I started to pay.
Here is pretty clear evidence of an understanding concerning the payment of money on condition that the wife left the home. In other words, once she had satisfied the husband that she had indeed left the domicile and had moved to Toronto he was prepared to pay the sum of $100 a month. It is evidence of this type which should cause members of the house to give very serious consideration to voting approval of this particular bill. I think my colleagues have brought out the point that when a petitioner comes before parliament for a divorce we should expect him to come with clean hands. I agree that, according to the rules governing the granting of divorces by parliament, that is not necessary. As a matter of fact, my understanding is that parliament can grant a divorce for any reason whatsoever. The matter is left purely to the discretion of the committee and, of course, eventually the members of parliament of both houses. While it may not be absolutely necessary as a matter of law for a petitioner to come before parliament with clean hands, I suggest that as a matter of practice we should require that in such cases.
Private Bills
Here is a case where a man is asking that the marriage be dissolved and the circumstances surrounding the whole case are such as to leave very serious doubts in our minds whether he deserves a divorce. Moreover, he admits having beaten his wife. When the question of the petitioner's conduct is brought up it is of course shied away from by suggesting that after all it is not the petitioner who is on trial, it is not his conduct that is under discussion but his wife's conduct.
My colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), brought out the very important point about the preference of the 14 year old girl. Here is a case where the sympathy of the child was with the mother, and I think that is something to which we should attach a great deal of weight. Therefore I am going to vote against the bill for the reasons advanced by my colleagues and particularly because I feel first of all that the petitioner has not come before parliament with clean hands and is not deserving of consideration by the members of this house. Second, I feel that the sympathy towards the mother evidenced by the 14 year old child must be given a great deal of weight. Third, I suggest that the whole circumstances surrounding this man's desire to get rid of his wife must be considered, particularly the fact that he went to the extent of entering into an agreement with her whereby if she left the home and moved away from Montreal he would pay her $100 a month. That does not seem to me to be a logical thing for a man to do who has been wronged in the manner in which he claims to have been wronged. Therefore I urge all members of the house to vote against this bill when the vote is taken.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one final objection at this stage. I realize this is the last opportunity I have to protect a 54 year old woman. I find it completely impossible to condemn a 54 year old woman to fend for herself for the rest of her days as best she can. As I indicated on second reading, I feel very strongly that the evidence is overwhelming that her husband agreed to pay her $100 a month if she would leave the home.
I welcome the fact that we have an aggressive new chairman of the miscellaneous private bills committee who is taking an active interest in these matters and participating in the debates. I think it will lead to greater efficiency and the methods followed will not be as slipshod as they may have been in other years. I should like to compliment him and express my high regard for the interest he has taken.

Private Bills
The point was raised that we have to let the bill go through because the respondent's lawyer apparently was satisfied. I have had many cases called to my attention where the respondent has not been made aware of her rights and does not know there is such a thing as the miscellaneous private bills committee of the house where her case can be reheard. Furthermore, as I stated in the other case, there is absolutely no arrangement with respect to the financial aspect of a rehearing before our committee.
The respondent's lawyer may have been satisfied but we are still not convinced that the respondent herself was satisfied. We are not convinced that she was even aware of what her rights are. The argument has been used in this case that we have no jurisdiction as to property rights. I agree that they fall within the authority of the provinces. However, I have yet to hear of the members of a jury or a judge rendering a verdict and condemning a person without considering the consequences of their verdict. I believe that as members of the House of Commons we must not only deal with each case on its merits but in rendering a decision we must be fully aware of what the consequences of such a decision are in all likelihood going to be.
We are going to ask this 54 year old woman to continue to live as best she can. While her health last's I suppose she may be able to continue her job as a dishwasher at $21 a week but what is she to do if her health does not remain good or if she loses that position? I think we have to bear that in mind. Above all, I do not think we should at this time exonerate the husband of all responsibility. There have been many arguments put forward on the question of the $100 a month. According to the lawyer this woman left the home on January 5, 1954 and when the husband testified he said, as found on page 14 of the evidence: "In March I start to pay the $100."
She left on January 5 and I say there is a clear indication that the woman's side of the story should at least be given the benefit of the doubt, if not believed altogether. I am very happy to associate myself with those who are unwilling to use parliament for the purpose of throwing a 54 year old woman out on the streets of Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two. In my opinion, if the house sees fit to pass the bill at this time it will surely do so with more than a twinge of conscience. I agree with the members who have spoken on the bill. Here we have a case where it has not been established that adultery has been committed. On the other hand, it has been
[Mr. Regier.l
established that the petitioner has been guilty of very great cruelty to the wife and practically drove her from the home by reason of his attitude and conduct. Through the questioning of counsel for the respondent it has been established that there is certainly a great deal of circumstantial evidence proving misconduct on the part of the petitioner. I think that we who have gone into the merits or demerits of this case have indicated to the house that there is doubt as to the authenticity of the evidence given by the petitioner and the investigators. Along with the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) I feel that here is a case in which, if we pass this bill, it is going to leave a comparatively young woman, one 54 years of age, to fend for herself. She has already indicated that she has been obliged to work as a dishwasher and to work in the tobacco fields. It may well be that the sorrow and the grief she has had through having been forced by a cruel husband to leave her home will be increased by the fact that she may not get the custody of her child. I think it is significant that this woman, under the circumstances that I have indicated, has kept this young girl with her for seven months out of ten. That fact would indicate that to some degree at least she should be entitled to more of an act of justice, might I say, than it seems to me we shall be providing her with if we pass this bill at this time and do not make provision that she at least can come before our committee of this house so that we may understand more fully the facts of the case.

speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 188, for the relief of Lois Margaret Clouston Willar.

Mr. Speaker, I notice a new principle is being established and I regret it very much. Until this year I believe these bills were considered on their merits, but I now see they are being looked upon as votes of confidence in the government. I regret that departure very much. Apparently, the Liberal party is now committed or during these past several votes has committed itself to the principle of agreeing to any and every divorce that may be put before the house for consideration. I notice that goes even far beyond what the hon. members of the other place are doing in that this year already they have refused a fair number of divorces. However, it seems

Private Bills
to be taken for granted that once the sanction of the other place has been given, this place is not to have any more authority in connection with these matters.
The Liberal party has now adopted a new principle, a principle of insisting on using their steam-roller vote to see to it that every one of these divorces passes this House of Commons. Those who may have conscientious objections are kind enough to the Liberal party, but unkind enough to their own convictions, to refrain from voting. They stay behind the curtain. I feel these matters should be put on the record. In addition to the many cases we get from Quebec, this one, as I said before, is from Newfoundland. Another principle seems to be finding root and receiving the sanction of the Liberal party and that is, if you live in Quebec and you want a divorce you must appear and present your case. Not only must you appear, but you must have with you other witnesses, and if you put forward a good case it will receive consideration and likely approval in both houses.
However, if you live in Newfoundland you have a special privilege. You do not have to show up at all and neither does the respondent have to show up. You do not have to send other corroborating witnesses. You have to send only one witness, and in some cases I notice it does not even have to be a witness now living in Newfoundland. Someone can be found living in Ontario who, at one time or another, may have been in Newfoundland and seen a man or a lady smile at someone of the opposite sex. This apparently is good enough for the parliament of Canada.
The other day some of us in committee wanted to have this case heard in a proper manner. Even though some of us do not agree that we are a court we believe we should conduct this business as it ought to be conducted, and would be conducted in any properly constituted court. We asked that the case be heard. We did not even admit that it had been heard, since there was only one witness called. The question was fired back at us, who is going to pay? Whose responsibility is it? When a committee of this House of Commons incurs an expenditure it is up to us to pay if the people are unable to pay. Surely, money is not going to be the thing that decides what the decision of a committee of this house is going to be.
We have never yet accepted that theory. On one committee last year we brought all kinds of witnesses from the city of Vancouver. We brought the chief of police and the warden of a jail and several others to testify before the committee. When it comes to calling witnesses from Newfoundland the question of who is going to pay arises. Aside from

the money question I also feel an important principle is involved here. If we are responsible members of this committee, or the highest court in the land if you call it that, we cannot afford to be accused of dissolving marriages without having at least one of the parties in the case appear before a committee of this house or the other place. I think that is another principle which is worthy of note. If this case and others like it are permitted to go through, my fellow citizens in British Columbia who are unsatisfied with local divorce laws should have the same right as loyal subjects of Her Majesty to petition this parliament if they are unsatisfied with conditions as they exist back home.
I would like to pose this question to the Liberal party: What will you do if you are swamped by 10,000 unsatisfied divorce applicants from one end of Canada to the other if neither party of any of the marriages has to appear? It is simply a matter of sending a penny postcard in order to apply for divorce.

Mr. Speaker, I would just like to say a few brief words. Since I came into this house I have never voted for a divorce bill but I have had sense enough not to decide how other people should vote and I have not presumed to tell them what their duty is. I am convinced that if we spent more time in attempting to remove the cause of divorce, which is cursed selfishness, we would be spending the taxpayers' money in a more constructive way.
I do not believe in divorce. That is my personal conviction because I do not want to be divorced from my better half. Should anyone try to cause trouble between my wife and me, he will get it in the neck as quickly as possible, by golly. The home is the bulwark of the nation and it is our duty to stand for the upbuilding of the home. If we do that we will cut divorce to pieces.
Mr. Speaker, I rise simply to object to the adjective "smutty" in reference to legislation before this house, as used by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) in his speech.

Mr. Speaker, since a new principle has been brought to the attention of parliament for the first time this afternoon I think we should look carefully at what we are about to do. If it is possible for citizens of Newfoundland to secure divorces without the petitioner or the respondent appearing, there is no valid reason why citizens of the province of Quebec should not have the same privileges. It is obvious that the bill will result in a drastic increase in the number of divorces if we extend to

the citizens of Quebec what we are apparently prepared to extend to the citizens of Newfoundland.
While apparently it is not a new practice, it is the first time it has been brought to my attention. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) has performed a valuable service in discovering this principle.
I notice that Mr. Burke-Robertson, a barrister residing in Ottawa, who handled this case, said:
I would like to ask leave to present the petitioner's case by affidavit. This is a Newfoundland case and it has been the practice on most of the other Newfoundland cases which I have had over the past few years to accept the petitioner's evidence by affidavit if the petitioner has no knowledge of the adultery which is alleged. In this case the petitioner can only prove the marriage and the domicile of the parties and is not able to give any evidence on the issue of adultery.
My attention has been drawn to the fact that another divorce was granted this year under similar circumstances wherein it was not necessary for the petitioner to put in an appearance. I think that is a new principle in dealing with justice where the welfare of men, women and children is involved. I certainly do not propose to give my consent to the granting of divorces on this sort of procedure.
Their Honours the senators were also a little uneasy. Senator Fergusson said:
Mr. Chairman, don't you think we should discuss that point in the main committee before deciding. We are acting as a subcommittee and we usually discuss such a matter in the main committee before taking affidavit evidence of any kind.
The chairman said:
Yes. We will adjourn for a few minutes in order to consult with the chairman.
Senator Roebuck, chairman of the main committee, joined the subcommittee and the barrister explained the procedure. Senator Roebuck added his comments.
I think that hon. members in this chamber should not remain silent; I think they should vote for or against a principle as far-reaching as the principle we are asked to establish in supporting the bill which is now before us. For my part, I would like to register my opposition.

speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the question should be put until we realize the meaning of the new principle which has been mentioned by the hon. members who have spoken. They have mentioned the Liberals in this house voting solidly. I do not think a new principle is involved here because as I understand
Private Bills
it we are always willing to assist those minorities which require assistance and privileges. Furthermore, since Canada stretches from one ocean to the other certain privileges should be granted to certain groups which would otherwise have a great deal of difficulty or would be deprived of the advantages other Canadian groups might have. If the people of Newfoundland by some chance happened to live in another province they could have divorces granted by supreme or county courts and the situation might be different. However, the people of Newfoundland, as Canadians, should have every privilege and opportunity in relation to the dissolution of marriage as other Canadians enjoy and this happens to be the procedure upon which their divorce rights are based.
Some question has been raised here about the procedure. If we examine the courts of Canada we realize that it is a pretty general principle. I think the courts of Canada are recognized the world over for their justice and integrity.
As a general principle, in some courts evidence can be presented by deposition which is not too much different from evidence in the form of an affidavit or a sworn statement. In divorce cases the petitioner can file certain affidavits with the Senate committee.

Mr. Speaker, this particular petitioner filed an affidavit in support of his petition and which is part of the evidence. This evidence was never questioned. He was domiciled in the province of Newfoundland and was married to the respondent on such and such a date. To bring him the distance it would be necessary to bring him when there is no dispute or presumption of dispute would probably cause more difficulty. If the case had been opposed I presume a request would have been made

Private Bills
to have brought persons before the committee to give evidence, but this petitioner could not add a* great deal to what was given before.
I believe in this case evidence was given by a 35 year old garage mechanic, not by a professional investigator of the type some of our hon. friends are worried about.
It was said that to adopt this type of procedure might result in a divorce bill passing by which a respondent might be divorced and not know he had been involved in a petition for divorce. I do not think there is much possibility of that happening because in Canada officers of the court serve all these documents. I understand that in this case service was made by a court officer who filed with the clerk of petitions an affidavit of service properly sworn before a notary public or someone authorized to take such affidavits.
There was corroboration which was completely independent and no objection was raised. It seems to me that the evidence in this case should be considered as being sufficient. It has been said that the Liberal party has voted solidly on this, but I have not noticed that in the past except when the facts and principles involved required it.
In conclusion I might suggest that if any party wishes to vote solidly against the principle as set out, that it is necessary to bring people from Newfoundland, the petitioner or even both parties although sometimes the respondent never turns up, that would be voting to bar the people of Newfoundland from the rights and privileges which they now have.
