maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I should like to spend a few minutes on this legislation and the amendment moved by the

hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I think a great deal of weight was given in the committee that considered the bill to evidence which possibly indicated that there was very little difference in the situation with respect to the further development of this railway than was the case ten years ago, when the company first approached the house for a franchise covering a period of ten years for the development of the road. In subsequent speeches that have been made on the subject I believe one salient feature has been overlooked, namely that at the present time the applicant for this franchise has lost the pioneering spirit which motivated it in carrying out the program that has been carried out thus far.
When the company approached the house for permission previously it had been making surveys in the area around Schefferville and had come up with indications of some valuable iron ore properties. It was obvious at that time that if it were to be in a position to carry out development work, a railway was definitely necessary.
Now the situation is that the railway has what it wants. It has a railway to its door, to its own properties. As I have indicated previously, there is not the same incentive to this particular company to carry out the further development work which will be required in order to push the railway forward to Ungava bay.
I think also that it is an extremely naive view that has been held in some quarters that this of course is not an exclusive franchise, that it is only some enabling legislation, and that if this particular company does not go forward with its plans then of course there will be plenty of opportunity for other companies to come forward, make an application and have their application dealt with on its merits.
That sounds very nice, Mr. Chairman, but from the practical standpoint I do not think there is any doubt about it that what we are handing over here today is an exclusive right for an additional 10 years. I would say this. If someone else came along in the interval and suggested that they would like to move in here and start extending this particular line of railway, I believe they would be quickly told no, that there was a company which had opened up the original area here and that they still had several years to go before they could be put out of the market in this connection.
There is this matter of the removal of incentive as far as going forward is concerned. On the other hand, there is every indication that the area now holds the same promise to the north that was there in the
Private Bills
original construction period of the rail line. I might refer to the examination of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra when he questioned the manager of the railway company. At page 20 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, we find the following:
By Mr. Green:
Q. When you showed the committee the small map you showed us a stretch of base metal territory running to Ungava bay and to the west of it a similar stretch of iron ore territory.-A. Yes, there is a possibility of finding enrichment in it. There has been a great deal of exploring done on the iron ore field apart from the low grade ore in the vicinity of Ungava bay.
Q. There are iron ore possibilities on the way north from Schefferville to Ungava bay?-A. I do not say somebody would not find an iron ore mine in between. The most central deposit of high grade ore which we have is about 50 miles northwest of Schefferville at a place called Eclipse.
The indication here is that somebody might find it, but there is not the same lure in front of this particular company to carry on this work. If the same pioneering spirit were developed by this company today, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me there would be no question about its ability to carry forward the necessary surveys, get the work under way and do it long before the expiration of the 10-year period that has been provided for in the application. I say that the amendment which has been made limiting this period to 5 years appears to be reasonable.
I may have been a little surprised in committee to find that some members of the C.C.F. party thought the 10-year period was quite all right. However, when I looked back at Hansard of the session of 1947, volume III, page 2437, I found there an indication that all their members did not feel that way. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has redeemed himself here by carrying on the same argument that he used at that time. I should like to quote what he said back in 1947:
Nevertheless, as I was saying when the minister interrupted me, this bill not only gives the company control over bus lines, transportation and all the rest of it which is included in the bill-if it is a provincial matter it should not be in the bill-but it definitely delegates these rights to the company. The worst feature of it, as I see it. is that the company is not obligated to begin operation of the road for five years, which can serve the purpose of keeping someone out if they want to go in and develop that territory in that time. If at the end of ten years the job is not completed, then, under the bill, the government has the right to rescind it. So far as the development of the resources and the railway line in there are concerned, it is definitely gone, because the company can do what they like with it for the next ten years. They are not obliged to do anything about it. The bill precludes anyone else from going in there and developing the area.

Private Bills
Those conditions still exist, I submit, Mr. Chairman. I believe that if the applicant in this case wants to show good faith and wants to continue the same pioneering spirit which it used previously, it should not object in any way to the reduction of this period from 10 years to 5 years.
There is one other feature about this matter, and it has been discussed in this house previously. Here again the control of a vast amount of the natural resources of this country is being handed over to people outside of this country. Someone may say it has been handed over by another legislative authority, but by this legislation dealing with the franchise for a railway which will probably be the only major means of opening up this territory I say that in this case again, this House of Commons is going to ensure that the control of thousands and thousands of acres of the best ground in this country from the natural resources standpoint is going to be handed over to interests which are entirely outside this country. There is again the feature that we are not paying attention to the essential fact that if we are not careful we are not going to control within our own country all the wonderful assets which have been left here for us.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad to say that I find myself in complete agreement with the opening remarks of the hon. member for York West wherein he stated something to the effect that there is little difference between the situation now and the situation 10 years ago in respect of this railway company; but probably my reasons for feeling that this is the case are somewhat different from his. I have been attempting to follow his remarks rather closely. I must say that I am rather clear in my mind as to what he is against in this connection, but I have little idea as to what he is for. I gather that for some reason or other he is opposed to this particular concern having a franchise to extend this railway, but he does not suggest what the alternative would be if this franchise is not granted.
I think my position today, Mr. Chairman, is the same as that which was taken by the hon. member for Cape Breton South 10 years ago, namely that this is the kind of development which should have been handled in a manner which would have kept its benefits in the hands of the people of Canada. I must say that I found it rather amusing, both in the house and during the committee hearings on this bill, to find the great Conservative party and its members raising all the fuss and furor that they have been raising about this particular bill at this particular time. There are occasions when they seem to pride

themselves as being the great champions of what they like to call free enterprise. Yet in this case they seem to have some particular gripe against this particular firm. I must confess that I have not yet discovered the reason for it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for York West indicated in the committee that he was in favour of private monopolies.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: He never said that.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: In my remarks in the committee I made it clear that if you were going to have a monopoly I would favour a public monopoly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member at this stage, but may I volunteer to him the information that the remarks he is now making are entirely in order on clause 1 and would be in order on clause 1 whether the amendment before us is carried or defeated. But I suggest to him that the line of thought he is pursuing, as to whether or not this particular company is to build the line, is not the question before the committee at the moment. The question before the committee at the moment is whether we shall continue the 10-year period or make it a 5-year period. Then we shall decide whether or not the clause shall be carried. I would ask hon. members at this stage to restrict their remarks to the subject matter of the amendment, because when the amendment' has been disposed of the clause will be open for discussion.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. Although I understand you are ruling some of the remarks out of order, I think in connection with the remark made about my statement on monopolies I might be allowed to read from page 28 of the committee evidence the actual words used.
If there is anything I don't like it is public monopolies. I like private monopolies little more-

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
At the risk of incurring your displeasure, sir, I might remark that I thought I was giving a reasonable paraphrase of that particular statement. However, Mr. Chairman, perhaps I have not made my point in connection with the amendment as clear as I might have. The precise point of the remarks I was making was that I am quite frankly puzzled as to why this amendment is before us, in view of the ideas put forward by the hon. member and his colleagues.
The position I took on this question in the committee when we were discussing an identical amendment moved there, was that this amendment was tantamount to telling this firm that they must commence construction

Private Bills
of this line immediately. However, there was no evidence in the committee that there was any immediate need for this particular railway line. There was no evidence that mining properties would be proved up and would require a railway line. There was no indication that there would be any other traffic except that originating from the mine to justify the construction of the railway beyond the point to which it has already been built. For that reason, I felt in the committee, and still feel, that regardless of whether this is going to be built by a private monopoly or a public monopoly-I agree with the hon. member for York West that in effect this is tantamount to an all-inclusive franchise so far as a railway in that area is concerned-the cost of this railway construction if it should prove to be an uneconomic venture is going to come back on the shoulders of the people of Canada. For that reason I indicated in the committee that I would have been much happier if the hon. member had proposed an amendment which would, in effect, have indicated to the company that they must commence construction within five years. I made it clear in the committee that I would have been prepared to support that kind of amendment.
Personally I cannot see that it is wise to compel this company, as this amendment in effect suggests, to commence immediately the construction of some hundreds of miles of railway line. Indeed, it has yet to be proven whether there is or ever will be any traffic for a railway to carry. However, the main question is whether or not this franchise should ever have been granted, or whether it is wise to extend a franchise for an indefinite period to large private monopolies. I think, Mr. Chairman, I have attempted to clarify my own position on this amendment. Perhaps I might not find it necessary to pursue the broader question when we come to consider clause 1, in view of the fact you believe I have covered a broad area in my discussion of the amendment itself.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
In introducing this amendment to the house, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has once again indicated a desire to rush into things for the sole purpose, in so far as the Conservative party is concerned, of hurrying up a program in order to bring these important matters to the attention of the public, indicating that they are a do-something party. I agree with the spirit of the amendment, the spirit being that there should be a railway extension into the northern part of Quebec and particularly from Knob Lake to Ungava bay. We cannot, however, go along with the suggestion that it must be built within a 5-year period.
I believe we have had sufficient evidence brought before the committee to indicate that it is quite impractical to expect this company to finish this job within a 5-year period. I do not see the justification for forcing the issue and having a railway line constructed over territory which will be non-productive. The line should not be built until such time as a request has been made by some responsible mining industry or some other responsible body and evidence is given to indicate that a rail line is necessary. As I understood the committee report, it was indicated that all that need be done was that certain representations be made to the railway company indicating that an extension of the line was desirable and necessary to get their products to market, and the line would be started.
Now, the fact that a rail line is necessary is certainly true but it is definitely not necessary to have that line constructed within a 5-year period, unless there is someone in that region who has a business enterprise, a mining industry, that would make it essential. I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni because I felt that he approached the problem in an extremely realistic way, which is something I really appreciate about the hon. member. In relation to this question, as in several other cases, I think the hon. member revealed a reasonable approach. We must face reality. We have a great north land which needs to be opened up. But to bind to a five-year period a company which has proven it is doing a good job in this particular area, or to take away its franchise, would be the height of folly.
In so far as statements concerning monopoly are concerned, I think the hon. member for York West made himself quite clear when he indicated that he did not like a private monopoly any better than he liked a public monopoly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: He said a little better.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: He did not say a little better; he said "little better", as I recall it, which to my mind means that he did not think there was much to choose between either of them. We have a board of transport commissioners for the protection of the public, which should regulate these things in respect to monopoly, either public or private. There is nothing defensible in either, I might add, if they are exploiting the public. However, Mr. Chairman, that is not the purpose of our present discussion.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
There are no public monopolies. There has never been any prosecution. There have been prosecutions on the other side.

Private Bills

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: The government cannot prosecute itself.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cape Breton indicates that there are no public monopolies. I probably should not have called them by that name. I should have said there are government enterprises; but try to get into business, such as the T.C.A., and you will soon discover for certain whether or not there are public monopolies.
I think I have made myself quite clear concerning the stand I take. I do want to see the development of the north land of Quebec, as part of the north land of Canada, but I do not expect it to happen in the next five years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this bill was discussed for the first time in this committee the other day, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra claimed that by granting the extension of 10 years asked for by the company, we would be placing a stranglehold on the district. This line of argument was to some extent taken up this afternoon by the hon. member for York West, when he contended that by this bill we were giving an exclusive franchise to the railway company for a further period of ten years.
I do not think it is necessary for me to repeat what has been said before in this connection both in this committee and in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; that is to say, that by this bill we are only amending the incorporating act of this company by providing that it shall have a further ten years starting in May, 1957, in which to carry out the whole undertaking envisaged by its incorporation. If some hon. members still persist in contending that we are placing a stranglehold on this district, one has only to remind them that if a stranglehold was ever placed on this district, it was when the mineral rights were granted to the mining companies in that district by the Conservative government of the province of Quebec.
Speaking on this question of mineral rights, I wish to remind hon. members that the Quebec Iron Ore Company is not the only company holding mineral rights in the district proposed to be served by this extension. At this point I wish to quote from the report of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, when Mr. Durrell was asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra to answer some questions. Mr. Durrell had this to say, as reported at page 15 of the report:
Between Leaf bay and the coastal area we have considerable holdings, and we are doing a lot of drilling; but we would hardly call it ore today. It would be if it were just outside Montreal; but we need large tonnage to justify an extension to the railway.
CMr. Gillis.)
In reply to a further question asked by the hon. member, as to whether these were iron ore deposits, Mr. Durrell had this to say:
No, base metal deposits, copper and nickel.
I asked a question, as reported at page 22 of the report:
Mr. Durrell, have you been requested by any of the companies holding mining rights north of SchefTerville for this extension?
In reply to my question Mr. Durrell answered:
No sir. We have not.
My contention is that the company is right in coming before this parliament and asking not to be called upon to proceed with this extension until such time as the ore deposits in the district have been proven and can be exploited. Even if it were proven today that these ore bodies were ready for exploitation, my contention is that the five-year extension of time proposed by the amendment would not be sufficient. This was also borne out by the evidence placed before the committee. Mr. Durrell stated quite clearly that it would take at least two or three years to complete the survey and to prepare the necessary plans.
Mr. Durrell also stated that it had taken over four years to build the first part of the project from Seven Islands to Schefferville. He added that this part of the line was built by expediting the work, by using airlift to quite an extent and by spending about twice the amount of money that would have been required to build this line under ordinary circumstances without rushing the construction. He also added that the terrain in the district north of Schefferville to Ungava bay was worse, as far as railway construction is concerned, than the stretch between Seven Islands and Schefferville. Therefore it can be safely said that it will take more than four years. Mr. Durrell gave evidence before the committee that it would take some six years more for the completion of this line. If we say to this company that they can have only five years in which to carry out the project, we will not be giving them sufficient time to even make a start on the construction. It is quite clear that the minimum of time required to complete the survey, to prepare plans and specifications and to build the line would be of the order of eight or ten years.
The other day the point was made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that this extension should have been undertaken by Canadian National Railways. I do not think it will be necessary to spend very much time to prove to the committee that this is not the type of project which should be undertaken by Canadian National Railways.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I interrupted another hon. member and asked him to remember that what we have before us is an amendment to reduce the period of the extension from ten to five years, and I do not think we should be discussing whether some other railway should be authorized to build this line.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I accept your decision. I was just answering the point made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I should like now to deal with the other point which was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra when moving his amendment. The hon. member said that this company should not be allowed to undertake this project because it is being financed chiefly in the United States. In reply I would say that I do not see anything wrong with a company of this kind being financed outside of Canada. I should like to quote what Mr. Durrell had to say before the committee about the financing of the company. In reply to a question by the hon. member for Edmonton East Mr. Durrell said:
Q. How do you intend to finance your line? Can you tell us?
A. We financed this line ourselves. We did not go to anybody for assistance. Out of the $255 million we have spent for capital expenditure, we borrowed $145 million from insurance companies. I regret to say that Canadian insurance companies were offered the first "crack" at it but unfortunately we only had four who would participate. They felt that the development of the north country was not properly justified so the bulk of our money came from American insurance companies. Canadian companies were offered the first chance. That was a blow to me. I am a Canadian.
To a further question by myself Mr. Durrell added that out of the total of $145 million which the company needed to borrow in order to complete the first section of the line, roughly $2 million had been advanced by Canadian insurance companies. If companies of this type cannot find the necessary finances in Canada to develop particular sections of our country, are we going to postpone the exploitation of our natural resources?
I submit that the amendment should be opposed because it does not give sufficient time to the company to carry out survey and other preliminary works, to draw up the plans and ,to complete the construction. I would remind hon. members that we are not giving the company ten more years to make up its mind, and in this connection I should like to quote the latter part of clause 1, which reads:
-and if within the said period the said line of railway is not completed and put in operation, the powers of construction conferred upon the company by the parliament of Canada shall cease
Private Bills
and be null and void as respects so much of the said line of railway as then remains uncompleted.
It is quite clear that we are not giving the company ten more years in which to make up its mind. It is being given ten more years in which to make the survey, build the line and put it into operation. If the company fails to do that within the period, it loses the powers conferred upon it by its charter. I submit that the ten years which will be given by the bill is not too long a time. It is barely time enough for the company to carry out the construction of this line, which I hope will soon be undertaken in order to develop this part of the province.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, following the last speaker may I say that this bill gives the company not ten years but eleven years, because the first ten years will not be up until more than a year from now. Not only does it give them another eleven years, it gives them control over a great land mass containing a tremendous mining potential and extending for 300 square miles in the northern part of that country. This company got a franchise in 1947 but they did not start to build the present line until 1949. They completed the line two and a half years ago to their own mine. The first section was built in a little over four years, and it is now proposed to complete the line to Ungava bay, an extension of about the same distance.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will give this company an extension of six years, which is nearly twice as long as it will take them to build this railway if they want to go at it right away. The vice-president of the company stated before the committee that they could build the line in less than four years, and he said also that they could do the survey work in two years. Therefore an extension of five years will give them a total of six years in which to complete this line of railway.
I object to any ten-year period being granted because it will tie up a large area of the country and leave it under the control of large American interests. Nobody will have a chance to go in there, find a mine and build a railroad. If somebody else wanted to build another line they would have to come back here and we would have to change this whole set-up. I have no objection to Americans coming here and spending their money and developing any part of our country, but I have objection to tying up a large mining area to United States interests for that period of time. There are other people participating there at the present time, but what if those companies set about getting franchises for a period of another ten years?

Private Bills
I think the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, giving them another five years, which is really six years from the present time limit, is giving them plenty of time. No matter what interests they have, we should not have a great area of our country tied up to large United States interests. We may have groups in this country who wish to open mines and develop some of their country. Surely we are not going to tie this country up so that somebody who is not a Canadian can go in there and develop a mine and build a railway, or even build an extension of a railway.
Five years is long enough. The evidence has proved that that is sufficient time to build this railroad. It gives them two years to make a survey, and it takes four years to build it. The evidence given in the railways, canals and telegraphs committee was that that was plenty of time. They said they could do it in less time than that if they were to fly stuff in, which would make more expense. Nobody is asking them to do that, to make extra expense; but when they have given evidence that they can do the job in six years, and we offer that after giving them one period of ten years, I think we have gone far enough and been fair enough with this company. Far be it from me to suggest that we stop this company from bringing in money to develop this country, but this is tying it up for too long a period.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Gaspe was working on the premise that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was attempting to end all work, that he did not want to see the railway go further, and that by putting a limitation on the time he was trying to frustrate the work of the company in proceeding further. That was not the impression I got at that time. My impression was that he thought five years was sufficient, following next year, 1957, to prove they were really in earnest about extending this railway to Ungava. So far as the evidence went, all the figures they gave showed that they could do it in that time.
Be that as it may, he said that if the extension were given for an extra five years, it would be up to the company to show something for that five years and then come back to the house and ask for a further extension, proving good faith and that they had made sufficient progress during that five years to warrant giving them the balance of the ten years. So it was beyond the comprehension of some members of the committee why they should be given that full extension. The amendment was to give them a five-year extension, which really meant six years, so

that if they came back after that time and showed that they had made sufficient progress on the work, then they would be given the balance.
What has the company been doing up to now? They have only started to make surveys and do the research work. As to progressing farther north, they have been standing still all that time. Now they advance the argument that they want another ten years. What have they done in that time? They have now built some 355 miles of railway. Surely the company has not been standing still all this time. They should have made sufficient plans and have made the necessary surveys so they could accomplish the best part of the work in the next four years.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I wish to make a few remarks in case the wrong impression has been given regarding the building of this railway. I think it would be well for the house to consider for a few moments just why the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company built a railway in the first place. They built a railway in order to transport ore from Knob Lake to an ocean port. As the Conservative speakers have pointed out, it has taken nearly nine years to build this railway and get it into a position where they could ship ore.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: It took them less than four years.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
It is about nine years now, and the railway has just come into operation and has not made any money as yet. Mr. Durrell told us in the committee that he hoped that, if the production this year was as they expected it to be, next year they would make a profit. These men collected $255 million to build a railway, and port, to open up an ore field. Therefore it was good, sound logic that they should build this line. There is no similar logic ito justify them in proceeding further at this time.
They asked for an opportunity to build a railway through to Ungava bay in case ore should be found farther north and it would be advantageous to have a seaport on the northern coast of Canada. If they found these ore fields, then they would be prepared to build this line. We were told in the committee that exploration work was being done in that area, and that at the present time there was no ore field that made it logical for them to proceed. They have shown good faith. They discovered an ore field and they built a railway.
This motion of the Conservative party is one to curb free enterprise. All through the committee proceedings the Conservative

members were saying that this should not be a free enterprise movement, that we must curb them, that the government must step in at the last minute and put curbs on it, after a group of men-four of this company's directors are Canadian and one American- had developed this section of the country for us. Let me say this. Of the $255 million that was raised to build this project, $143 million was raised in the United States. I should like to read Mr. Durrell's comment on how that money was spent. He said they had some difficulty at the start, and they had to buy cars from the United States. Then he went on to say this, as recorded on page 24 of the evidence:
Since then we have been buying almost 100 per cent Canadian, and in the $255 million I do not think probably more than 5 per cent went out of the country.
It is all very well for the Conservatives to suggest that it is a bad thing to borrow money from the United States, but when these people themselves borrow and raise $255 million and all of it but 5 per cent is spent to give labour in this country of ours,
I think it is a very good thing to go outside and borrow some money in order to give employment here. It is a sorry thing for this country when the great Conservative party takes an attitude adverse to such development-

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Nobody said they did not want them to borrow.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: You accused them of being a United States company.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I did not.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: There is only one director from the United States in the whole company. I want to say this-and I would like anyone else who disagrees with me to comment on it-that if and when there is an ore body of commercial value, this company will build an extension, the same as they have built a railway from Seven Islands to Knob Lake. They will handle the new ore, and no government should give people who invest money the feeling that the minute they get into this position then someone would take it away from them. This should not be done.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
We are engaged now in a discussion of the first clause of this bill, which reads, in the first few lines of paragraph 1, as follows:
Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company, hereinafter called "the company", may within a period of ten years from the 14th day of May, 1957, complete that portion of its line of railway authorized by chapter 80 of the statutes of 1947 which is not now completed . . .
The amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is to the effect that
Private Bills
the word "ten" be struck out and "five" substituted therefor. The purpose of the amendment is not to raise an obstruction to the building of a line of railway for opening up a section of the northern part of Canada where mineral development may be carried on. That is not the purpose of the amendment. It is not intended to be obstructionist, because we are just as interested as anyone else in the development of Canada's great north.
However, I think anyone looking at this matter very closely would see that to grant an extension for a period of ten years as requested by the company, when they still have one year to go on the old charter, would give them more than ample time for any purpose they might have in mind. A five-year extension would be more in line with the progress that is being made in Canada at the present time. It seems to me that in 1947, nine years ago, when the charter was granted, and a ten-year period was put in the legislation, the situation in the development of Canada's mineral wealth was very different from what it is today. In 1947 we were not aware that we were going to have the great development that has occurred since that time. In 1947 we were not aware that the resources of the North American continent were being depleted at the rate shown by the subsequent Paley report.
Consequently the whole picture of mineral development in the Canadian north land is materially different from what it was in 1947 when the ten-year charter was granted. This company was entering into unknown territory. It had to make extensive surveys and it was difficult to get started although, by reason of the airlift, the job of building the present railway was completed rather quickly. The airlift and the rapid construction of the railway coincided with the pressing demand for iron ore and were timed to coincide with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.
I think the ten-year period allowed in 1947 was reasonable under the circumstances prevailing at that time, and a five-year extension now would appear to be reasonable in view of the circumstances now prevailing. We are now in a sphere of development that is much more pronounced than it was ten years ago, and there is a much greater demand for our mineral wealth than ten years ago. Many more companies are interested in surveys and in searching for ore bodies. It seems to me that under these circumstances the company, if it is given a five-year extension of its present charter which in effect would give it six years to make up its mind, should have ample time for any extension of the railway line.

Private Bills
In reading some of the evidence given in the committee and subsequently quoted in the house I have noticed that when questions were asked of Mr. Durrell as to whether he felt justified in commencing construction of the extension at the present time he gave this answer, as quoted at page 2241 of Hansard of March 16:
There is nothing at the moment to justify the construction of a railway. Surveys show areas which may be suitable for mining development, but so far, as I said, we know of nothing which would justify beginning construction.
Reading further along in the evidence I see that there does not appear to be any great haste to start work in the minds of the proponents of the scheme. Is that why a ten-year period is required? If the railway is so desirable it would appear to me that immediate action would be necessary, and that survey work would be under way at the present time. After all, these people have a base of operations now which they did not have ten years ago. They have a railway line running up from the coast. They have experienced people and the experience they gained in laying that railway line. I would think their surveying of the next strip would be more rapidly done and more easily accomplished than in the case of their initial venture at the time they decided a railway line should be built.
All things being considered, the proposed extension of five years would grant them ample time to reach a conclusion. It is a strange thing. I noticed that the hon. member for Gaspe drew our attention to the latter part of the clause, which is to the effect that if the company does not complete the said line of railway and put it into operation, its powers will cease and be null and void in respect of so much of the said line of railway as remains uncompleted at the end of the ten-year period.
On the face of it that appears to be a restriction on the railway, but when you look at it a second time it may be a disadvantage to Canada. They might construct two or three miles of railway, let it rest for ten years and then quit on the job. There is nothing that compels them to complete the entire length of the railway within the ten-year period. It is far better to have a five-year settlement of the whole issue.
If development in mineral production proceeds during the next five or six years at the same rate as it has during the last five years, surely the pressure for a railway extending along the route herein proposed will become great within the next year or two and the company might then very well proceed; but as matters appear at the moment the company is asking for an extension of

its franchise for a ten-year period with great uncertainty whether anything is going to be done within that period.
I submit that within five years we might find it was urgent that something be done, might then be placed in the position that the company had not made the surveys, and delay would ensue. If it is as important as we are led to believe by those who have already spoken in favour of the measure, I fail to understand the statement of Mr. Durrell that "there is nothing at the moment to justify the construction of a railway." Why then attempt to gain control over this area without any decision that the extension of the railway is going to be proceeded with?
The hon. member who just preceded me- I refer to the hon. member for Wellington South-was suggesting that the Conservative party was opposed to the use of United States capital to develop the resources of this country. I think that is a wrong assumption or a wrong statement for anyone to make. We are not suggesting that foreign capital has not been useful in the past or that it will not be useful in the present and in the future. All we have suggested up to the moment is that full opportunity be given the Canadian people to exploit their own resources.
I was considering this question of delay brought forward in the evidence before the committee in the speeches of supporters of this bill, having regard to the fact that three years are required for survey and then another five years to build the railway. I think that is rather slow work under modern conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know the country at all?

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I have not seen that exact piece of country, but it is part of the Canadian north land and I have seen a great deal of that. I presume it is rocky and extremely difficult country in which to build railways. It may have muskeg for all I know. I do not doubt for one minute that it is extraordinarily difficult to construct a railway in that country. But I have travelled over various parts of Canada in which railways have been constructed with great difficulty, and I am not altogether unaware of the terrain of the Canadian shield in various parts of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Does the hon. member know that on the construction of this line between Seven Islands and Schefferville worse difficulties were encountered than in the construction of the railways across the Rockies?

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Did they have to build those spiral tunnels to construct that portion?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: If you read the evidence given before the committee, you will learn what those difficulties were.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I would think that spiral tunnels presented a greater obstacle than anything from Seven Islands up. I admit that it is not an easy task to build a railway in such territory, but modern methods of construction are much advanced over what they were many years ago, and modern methods of survey are perhaps much advanced over what they were years ago. We have air transport to assist in moving in materials and supplies, a procedure which would cut the time greatly.
When the C.P.R. was being built around the shore of lake Superior, supplies were ferried in by water and the time for construction of the railway was cut by five years by virtue of that fact. The line could have gone through less difficult country north of lake Superior, but it would not have been so easily accessible for the transportation of supplies.
Let us take for granted all these difficulties. Let us take it for granted that there may be difficulties in surveying and in building the railway line. It still does not follow that a full period of ten years is needed for that purpose. In any case, what is to prevent the company from coming back here and asking for another extension of time? If it shows that it has done the work, that the mineral bodies are there and that the development should proceed, there is nothing to prevent that company from coming back, receiving a fair hearing here and getting an extension such as it might require at that time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit another question?

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: How can he expect this company to finance such a project under the circumstances he just mentioned?

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I think that would be possible, just as has been done with the line it has already built. It is starting with an assured line to an assured ore body at the present time. Now it wants to extend that line up further into country where it is hoped that there are equally valuable mineral deposits.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: It is only a hope.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Until that hope is realized by exploration and so on, why the great haste to get an extension of ten years? Why not an extension of five years? If in that interval exploration indicates the existence of ore bodies of great extent and that a line can
Private Bills
be built without too great difficulty; and further, if the company shows that a five-year period is not adequate for that purpose, something might be done. On the other hand, if a very important body of ore is discovered there and it is urgent to get it out quickly, why not use another airlift as was done in the first instance and as was indicated here? Mr. Durrell said that is what they had used on this first section and that it was expensive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: It cost them double.

maintopic: QUEBEC NORTH SHORE AND LABRADOR RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
It might well be expensive for the proposed extension that is now in their mind, but it does not preclude the possibility of using an airlift to accomplish that purpose. Within a few years it may well be that the development of air transportation will have proceeded to an extent where it may be cheaper to conduct an airlift than it was in the period of construction of the present railway line.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the reasons we are suggesting that our amendment should receive careful attention and should be carried. A five-year extension, under present circumstances and with present development in our north country, should be ample for a decision to be reached as to when the line should be built and how it should be constructed.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
