We in this group are completely opposed to the passage of this bill, Mr. Speaker. We think there is no need for the change in the name; in fact the suggested change of name from Personal Finance Company to Beneficial Finance Company is a change that would inevitably mislead potential borrowers and is something that this house should oppose and reject.
A number of hon. members have objected from time to time to the type of advertising that is used by these companies in an attempt to drum up business. References have been made to the type of advertising used by this particular company, and in this respect I think the company is a very bad offender, because in my opinion it has put out a number of very misleading pamphlets. A number of these have been referred to me. One is entitled, "You Are My Pal"; another one, "Take This Good Friend On Vacation With You". The third one is a card on credit for extra fast service. There are other instances of this type that one might mention. I had another advertisement referred to me as an example of misleading advertising, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, March 21. I do not know if the company specified where the advertisement was to appear, but it was taken from the comic page. The advertisement is entitled, "The Happy Answer to Your Money Needs". It reads:
Question:	How can I pay up my bills and
reduce my monthly payments at the same time?
Happy Answer: Tell your money needs to Pacific Finance. The manager can give you good financial advice, can often reduce your monthly payments by as much as one-half-
Misleading, I would say at that point, -while paying off your bills, and can often give you extra cash besides.
The happy answer, get $25 to $2,500, Pacific Finance Credit Limited.
Then there is a list of the offices the company has in this city. One should keep in mind-
What has that to do with this company?

It is the same type of advertising. I am bringing this forward as an example of the type of advertising engaged in by these small loans companies which misleads the public. It is bad enough that this type of advertising is used, but it is allowed,
[The Deputy Chairman.]
we expect as an expense of the company in filing income tax returns. Not only do the borrowers have to pay large sums by way of interest because of this tremendous advertising campaign engaged in by the various companies, but because such large sums are allowed by the income tax people for advertising the general public obtains a smaller amount from these companies in the way of taxes. So, in fact, the public of Canada, by our income tax laws, are bonusing and paying half the cost of the advertising engaged in by these companies.
When we take part in the debates in this house, as we are doing now and as we did a year ago, some of us accuse these companies of misleading advertising. What did the companies do or what have they done? Niagara Finance, in answer to some of this criticism, has printed a book. Amongst other things the foreword says:
On the other hand, our industry has been the target for unjustified criticism-
I suggest that is a definite reference to statements made by members of parliament last year.
-by uninformed people-
Another slur.
-who have never felt the need for, nor used, the service provided by companies such as ours. Let us therefore, together, try to form an honest appraisal of the function of this industry in our Canadian economy, its usefulness and its business problems.
After having said it wants to form an honest appraisal, it makes statement after statement that is misleading, ill-founded and in some cases completely false. I think a quick reference to some of the statements in this book can prove that very statement. Not only has the company sought by this means to criticize, I suggest, statements made by members of parliament, but it is using this means to make unfounded and unwarranted attacks on the credit unions of this country. It does so in the following terms. It says of credit unions:
Such organizations are often formed in large plants, factories, or among social or community groups. They have the advantage of being run by the members, and their administration and other costs are therefore low.
Listen to this.
They contribute virtually nothing to the public treasury. They have comparatively no taxes to pay . . .
They can offer low rates of charge only because they are tax-free-
I suggest the statement made by this finance company that credit unions are tax-free is completely and wholly false. The laws of this country provide the same type of taxes, the same rates of tax, to all companies,

be they credit unions or be they finance companies. If a finance company wants to take advantage of the laws of this country as they are applied to all companies, all they have to do is pay out some of their inflated profits to the borrowers on the basis of a patronage refund as is done by the credit unions, and they will have levied on them precisely the same rates of tax as are levied on the credit unions. The law is applied equally to all companies. The reason the credit unions, of course, in practice pay a lower rate is the fact they return by way of patronage dividends to shareholders and to borrowers a substantial part of the profits that are made.
Then a little bit further along they make this statement:
The charge presently stipulated by our federal laws is 2 per cent per month on the outstanding balance of a loan to $500.
This statement is false because the federal law does not stipulate and does not set the interest rate at 2 per cent per month. It does not force these companies to charge 2 per cent per month, which is the direct inference from this statement. The law merely says the companies cannot charge more than 2 per cent. Then this pamphlet says:
If you conclude that this is an interest charge of 24 per cent you are in good company, for thousands of people believe the same thing.
Then they try to prove that it is less than 24 per cent, but I make the statement that 2 per cent per month is not 24 per cent, it is over 26 per cent per year. The rate that is allowed these companies as the law exists today is the tremendous rate of over 26 per cent per year.
My great objection is that these companies can make this kind of advertising in answer to statements made in this house, and I suggest will claim the cost of such pamphlets as part of their deductions for income tax purposes. The company was not content with issuing this pamphlet, but gave wide distribution to a number of advertisements in the Financial Post. These advertisements are just as misleading as the pamphlets from which I have quoted. There are four in the series, and one says:
It takes time for staff to fill out necessary forms, check credit, do the accounting, follow delinquent payments, discuss and sometimes rearrange loans. And time costs money. To cover these costs the mark-up really should be (but is not) as high as 27 per cent on the smaller loans, ranging down to 19 per cent on the larger amounts.
The statement they say is not correct is, in fact, quite correct, because the rate is over 26 per cent per year.
The millions of Canadian dollars loaned to the tens of thousands of Canadians who enjoy our service is evidence, we think, that they, too, consider our charges fair and just.
Private Bills
In other words, if people are forced to go to these companies and pay this exorbitant rate of interest, then according to the company and the advertisement that is an indication that thousands of Canadians support their business and approve of the extremely high charge. I could go on to cite many other instances of this same type of misleading advertising and straight propaganda that the government allows as a deduction from income.
I think we should stop the passage of this bill. I think we should stop the passage of any further bills to encourage more finance companies to begin operating at this time. These people are engaged in what is in effect legalized robbery. They have become parasites in our communities. They are thriving on the low income earners, and are obtaining exorbitant profits. Until a thorough inquiry is made by this house and the banking and commerce committee, I suggest that if we are to do our duty we should ask the sponsor to stand this bill at least until the banking and commerce committee has had an opportunity to look into the field of small loans companies to see if in fact there is a good argument for the passage of this particular bill, which I suggest there is not.
The operation of the small loans companies is not affecting just the ordinary Canadian who might come to one's mind, but is affecting the personnel of our armed services, the army, navy and air force personnel. According to their own records, in many cases these people are getting into trouble with the small loans companies and are in fact paying these huge rates of interest, and are thus becoming a problem for the benevolent funds in the various services.
I have in my hand a statement put out by the army benevolent fund. This is in the form of a memorandum circulated among various servicemen concerning this problem. What does it say? It says:
The extensive use of consumer credit and the mismanagement of family income are closely related. Accordingly, it is understandable that the financial welfare problems in Canada have increased proportionately with the increase of more than 100 per cent in personal loans, instalment contracts and other household borrowing in the past five years.
It then goes on to say that these people made a survey of the number of low income families who are in debt, and they report the following:
Average debts of $850 per family.
The amount being allocated from income for interest and service charges every month is between $10 and $16 (or 5 per cent to 8 per cent of the total pay).
According to this survey 5 to 8 per cent of the total pay of service personnel is being

Private Bills
used for the payment of interest to small loans companies. The report goes on to say:
This would seem to indicate the need for an educational program designed to assist the householder regarding the planned expenditure of family income and the proper use of credit.
Let us look at the position we are getting into. By way of estimates and legislation the government asks parliament to pass appropriations for the pay of our service personnel. After we have provided them with a certain level of income, this government proposes measures to set up small loans companies and to facilitate the small loans racket in order that loan sharks can get our service personnel in their clutches and force a great deal of embarrassment upon the service personnel themselves, upon their families and upon the army benevolent fund.
I suggest it is the duty of the government not only to make provision for the payment of our service personnel, but also by way of legislation to prevent these sharks from taking advantage of persons who have to borrow money.
The government pays our service personnel. The Liberal party comprises the government of this country. And then Duncan MacTavish, the president of the national Liberal federation, becomes a director of one or two small loans companies and he and his companies and the policies they are following are embarrassing our army personnel according to the survey and the statement of the benevolent fund.
Oh, oh.

I can understand the jeers of the Liberal members. I can understand that the Liberal members are very uncomfortable. Nevertheless I am suggesting to them that it is a fact that the policy they have allowed, the policy that is being followed by the small loans companies, the largest of which has on its board of directors the president of the national Liberal federation, is embarrassing our service personnel. This policy is making it difficult for the army benevolent fund to function, to the point that the benevolent fund has had to start an educational program in order to protect the service personnel of the country from the loan sharks, whose practices are condoned by this government and the legislation for which is provided by this government.
I suggested that if hon. members of this house are to do their duty not only to the public generally but particularly to our service personnel, we should block the passage of this particular bill.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words

about the bill which is now before the house. When the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Lefrancois) introduced the bill it seemed relatively simple and clear. He explained that this is a bill to change the name of the Personal Finance Company of Canada to the Beneficial Finance Company of Canada.
The Personal Finance Company of Canada is a subsidiary of the Beneficial Finance Company of the United States. He explained that the Canadian company wished to change its name to Beneficial in order that it would have a name similar to its parent company. It is difficult to think of any more adequate reason that could be advanced for a company coming to this house and asking for a change of name.
In connection with the authorized capital of the company he explained that the company was incorporated in 1933 with an authorized capital of $1 million. That was 23 years ago. The company now comes to this house and asks to increase its authorized capital to $10 million. The authorized capital of $1 million is all issued and outstanding. The company has had $9,350,000 paid to it as paid-up surplus. It now asks to have the capital increased to $10 million. Does that not seem a reasonable request?
What has happened in this debate? Three hon. members of the C.C.F. party have opposed the bill. I tried to look at their reasons for doing so calmly and dispassionately, in an effort to ascertain exactly what was the real reason the C.C.F. members opposed this bill. I came to the conclusion that the real objection lies in the fact that they dislike the small loans business as it is carried ' on under the law of Canada today. This company happens to be a company engaged in the small loans business and that is the basis of their opposition to this bill.
I suggest to the hon. members that that is a completely invalid reason for opposing this legislation. If hon. members do not like the legislation dealing with small loans the proper place to attack that legislation is when Bill No. 51 is before this house. Bill No. 51 is designed to reduce the rate of interest which can be charged by small loans companies, and when that bill is before the house hon. members will have an opportunity to express their views on the small loans business. But I suggest that in their endeavour to attack the Personal Finance Company of Canada they are unfair and discriminatory. If they want to attack the small loans business, let them do it at another time and place but not on this bill.
Hon. members of the C.C.F. party have been critical of the advertising carried on by small

loans companies. I suggest that there is a proper time and place to attack that advertising if hon. members do not like it, but when we are discussing this bill it is not the time and place. The hon. member for Assiniboia has referred tonight to some of the advertising used by some of those companies, but none of it was by Personal Finance Company.
Oh, yes; three out of the four documents I referred to were used by Personal Finance Company.

I think the hon. member referred to Pacific Finance Corporation and Niagara Finance Corporation, but I did not hear him refer to-I withdraw that. Whatever the hon. member may have said about advertising, even that carried on by Personal Finance Company, this is not the time to deal with it. That advertising is done in accordance with the laws of Canada. There is nothing illegal about it. If the hon. member thinks the law ought to be changed, the proper time and place to do that is when Bill No. 51 is before this house.
If I may I should like to deal for a moment with the reasons why the hon. members are opposed to this bill and to the name "Beneficial" being granted to this company. I think it is nothing more or less than the belief of the hon. members that the business carried on by Personal Finance Company is not beneficial in any sense to its customers, and therefore they contend that the name would be misleading and should not be granted. May I say that whenever an incorporated company applies to this house for permission to change its name, the name is always cleared. In the case of this company the name had to be cleared with the superintendent of insurance, who is in charge of the administration of small loans companies. There is a well known procedure with the companies branch of the Department of the Secretary of State to clear names.
The general principle is that an applicant can have any name he desires, with certain exceptions, such as the use of the word "Royal" and certain others, and provided that the name is not used by any other company or so similar to the name of any other company as to be calculated to deceive. In this case the superintendent of insurance has said that he has no objection to the name "Beneficial" being granted to this company, and the companies branch of the Department of the Secretary of State has raised no objection to the name being granted. I put this question squarely to hon. members of this house. Is the choice of a name going to depend upon the likes, the dislikes or the whims of members of this house? If a person wants to know whether he can use a certain name must 67509-1C6
Private Bills
he first poll the members of parliament to see what are their likes or dislikes?
What about the Queen Elizabeth hotel?

I do not want to get drawn away from my argument, but let me say that the name "Queen Elizabeth" was chosen by the Canadian National Railways. I do not know what procedure they went through before they adopted that name, but that case is different from this. The type of case I am talking about is one where an application is made to this house for the incorporation of a company, or a change of name, and I suggest that the only basis upon which it can be determined what name is available to the company is the basis which has prevailed in the past, that is to clear with the Department of the Secretary of State and the superintendent of insurance. If there is no objection, then the name should be granted.
In the speech which he delivered a few days ago the hon. member for Assiniboia referred to some advertising put out by small loans companies which began with "You are my pal", and he said he had it on good authority that this was advertising of small loans companies, but whether inadvertently or intentionally I notice that he did not say specifically that this advertising was used by the Personal Finance Company of Canada.
If the hon. member had inquired from the sponsor of the bill he would have been notified that this was not one of those advertisements that had been used by Personal Finance Company. The hon. gentleman waves his hand in that incredulous fashion that he uses so often, but the hon. member is not the only one in this house who tells the truth. I suggest to hon. members that the sponsor of this bill has been so informed by Personal Finance Company of Canada, and I submit that their statement should be accepted. I suggest that it would have been only a courtesy if the hon. gentleman had asked the sponsor about this before he put the advertising before the house. He should have asked whether that was one of the advertisements used by this company.
The hon. gentleman also made a great deal of the credit card issued by Personal Finance Company of Canada. The hon. member read from that card and made reference to the use of the words "Beneficial loan system". The hon. member went on to say that this indicated that the Personal Finance Company of Canada had adopted the name "Beneficial" which was an affront to this house.
I should like to point out that the Beneficial Finance Company in the United States is the parent company of a number of subsidiaries in the United States, and also of Personal

Private Bills
Finance Company of Canada. Was it not perfectly proper to use the word "system" in referring to a group of companies in the United States and a subsidiary company in Canada? I cannot comprehend how it would be an insult to this house to refer to what is a fact.
In addition, I am advised that this card was used long before there was any thought of making an application to this house for permission to change the name of the company to Beneficial Finance Company. The hon. member made considerable of the use of those words on the card, but I would like to point out that those words are in ordinary print. Then across the bottom of the card in large letters are the words "Personal Finance Company of Canada". No one could think that Personal Finance Company of Canada was using any other name but its own, and the hon. gentleman certainly stretched things a bit when he tried to convey to this house that this company had used the name "Beneficial" before the matter had been dealt with in this house.
May I just deal for a moment with the application to increase the capital of the company from $1 million to $10 million. I have already mentioned that the whole of the $1 million authorized capital has been issued and is outstanding. The company, in addition, has been using in Canada $9,350,000 of paid in surplus that was paid to them by the parent company in the United States.
For all practical purposes, that $9,350,000 is just as much capital as the $1 million. That is, the company has been using over $10 million of capital in the conduct of its business. The hon. member for Assiniboia professes a desire to see the real relationship between the earnings of the company and the capitalization of the company. The best way to grant his desire is to enable this company to increase its authorized capital to $10 million, so they can declare $9,350,000 of paid in surplus as a part of their capital. Then you will see that the capital used in this company is actually $10 million and not $1 million, and then you can balance up the earnings of the company against the $10 million capital used. I suggest that is the only way you can get a proper relationship.
Objection has been taken to increasing the capital on the grounds that Personal Finance Company in Canada is a wholly owned subsidiary of Beneficial Finance Company in the United States. What that means, as I understand it, is this. The hon. members object to a situation where a United States company has brought $10 million into Canada, borrows money from the bank to conduct its

operations, and may pay out dividends to the United States corporation. If that is a valid objection for Personal Finance Company of Canada, it is a valid objection for every other business carried on in Canada in similar circumstances. If it is an invalid objection for every other company, it is also an invalid objection for Personal Finance Company of Canada.
Now let me turn for a moment and apply that principle to other businesses in Canada. Let us take the Aluminum Company of Canada. It is a wholly owned subsidiary of the Aluminum Company of the United States. The development at Shawinigan and the development at Kitimat have been carried on largely by the moneys brought into Canada from the parent corporation in the United States. In turn that money will be used in Canada, and if need be the dividends will be paid to the United States corporation. Is there anybody in this house who is going to suggest that what has happened is anything less than a boon to the Canadian economy?
Some of the members of the C.C.F. party shake their heads at this argument. With due respect, it seems to me a perfectly sound argument. If I might reiterate, they object to this bill because this company is controlled by a United States corporation and is going to use this money and is possibly going to pay dividends to the United States corporation. The Aluminum Company of Canada is in precisely the same position in so far as capital is concerned and in so far as dividends are being paid out to the United States corporation. There is not a scrap of difference.
Now let me take another case. Let us take the field of oil development in Alberta. We know that one of the companies that has been foremost in development in Alberta and Saskatchewan has been the Imperial Oil Company of Canada. It is said that it had spent between $20 million and $30 million in exploration before it found a producing field. The Imperial Oil Company is a subsidiary of Standard Oil of New Jersey in the United States. The direct investment of United States capital in Canada in non-metallic minerals in 1945 was $133 million. In 1954 it was $586 million. That money has come into Canada from parent companies in the United States.
I want to be honest with the house. I do not say that the whole of the $586 million has come in connection with oil. However, is there anybody in this house who will say that what has happened in Alberta and Saskatchewan has not been good for Canada? If what has been done in these other fields has been good for Canada, can it be bad for Canada when applied to the Personal Finance Company of Canada? [DOT]
That is your gas pipe-line speech.

My submission is that you cannot brush aside with laughter arguments that are sound. The hon. gentleman had an opportunity to make a speech himself. If hon. members opposite do not think the argument I am putting forward is perfectly sound, I am sure that hon. members on this side of the house will be glad to hear what they have to say.
May I just say in conclusion that this is an application by a private company for relief applicable to itself. We are not concerned at this time wih the merits or demerits of the small loans business. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has stated that there is a legitimate place for the small loans business in the Canadian economy. He praised the work done by the Canadian Bank of Commerce and the credit unions, but he said that the rate of interest being charged by the small loan companies is too high. It will all be considered when Bill No. 51 comes before the house. My respectful statement to the house is that this is not the time or place for us to embark on a discussion of the merits or demerits of the small loans business. I suggest, with great respect, that this bill is clear. The relief sought is reasonable, and this house should approve this bill.

Private Bills
prosperous can go to the banks and borrow at a nominal cost. These people need it more than those who borrow at 4 or 5 per cent.
I mention this because all the evidence before the house is that these companies are growing in number, growing in strength, influence and power and growing financially. If we are going to allow this rot to get into our financial system we will have the condition that the people of Europe have tried to avoid for generations and still have with them. I suggest in all sincerity that we should be alarmed at the growth of these small loans companies and their immense profits. It indicates to me that something is rotten in our economy, and we as members will be remiss in our duties if we do not oppose the bill and all similar ones.
I am not against this particular company;
I am opposed to the whole principle of small loans at 24 per cent. I think they are inhuman and unchristian. I sincerely hope the government will take steps to investigate this avenue of borrowing which is keeping people down in the lowest depths of slum life. It is something in which we should be interested, something we should fight, and this is the time to start fighting. To charge a rate of 24 per cent to a man who is in debt already and has a small salary and a large family is inhuman. We have done nothing about it, and if we pass this bill we are simply aiding and abetting those who prey on the poor people of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. Just before I recognize the next hon. member, after listening to the last two speeches I think it is perhaps my duty to point out to the house that we are not debating Bill No. 51, I believe it is, which deals with the principle of small loans companies^ I would ask hon. members not to extend this debate to the whole field of the duties and responsibilities of the government respecting small loans companies as such, but to remember that the bill we have before us deals with whether or not certain amendments shall be made to the incorporating act of one company.
I am not suggesting for a moment that any argument for or against the passage of the bill with its two proposed amendments is objectionable because I am willing to listen to such arguments, but a discussion of the abstract question of the duty and responsibility of the government with respect to controlling our dealings with small loans companies is another debate now going forward in the house, and I would ask the house to try to keep this debate in order.

Mr. Speaker,
I want to say a few words before the vote is taken. It probably will not be taken tonight,

but I should like to have my words on the record before the vote is taken. We in this group are prepared to support the amendment, chiefly on two grounds. First of all, we do not think it either necessary or desirable that the name of this company should be changed from "Personal" to "Beneficial". The word "beneficial" is hardly the correct name to use for a company doing the type of business this company is doing. Surely no one will suggest for one minute that there can be anything beneficial in so far as the patron is concerned in having to pay 2 per cent a month for the money he borrows. It may be beneficial, of course, so far as the company itself is concerned, but so far as the person who borrows is concerned there is nothing beneficial in the transaction at all.
I do not think there is any doubt that one of the reasons the name is being changed is that the new name would be more attractive. I realize that the parent company may have the name "Beneficial", but just because the parent company has the name "Beneficial" is no reason why its offspring in this country should have to have the same name. We think it would be far better for them to continue to use the name under which they have been operating in the past.
As to the second point, that the capital should be increased from $1 million to $10 million, there again we are opposed for a number of reasons. In the first place, the intention must be for the company to expand its business. It will probably mean they will expand the number of branches throughout the country. There is one other large company, Household Finance, I believe, that has 160 branches altogether. No doubt this company will also increase the number of branches. Some members may argue that will be beneficial to the people because if you increase the number of offices it will increase competition, and if you increase competition the cost to the borrower will be reduced, but that is not the record.
Apparently the record is that where you increase competition in the course of carrying on a business of this kind and you go beyond a certain point, you actually increase the cost to the borrower. Some members will recall that was explained in the banking and commerce committee by the superintendent of insurance, Mr. MacGregor, in so far as insurance was concerned. He pointed out that when you increase competition beyond a certain point you increase greatly the cost of doing business because the advertising cost is increased. These companies are already doing a lot of advertising and the more companies you put into operation the greater the competition will become and the greater will

be the amount of advertising those companies will have to do. That will increase costs; therefore from the point of view of borrowers there will be nothing beneficial to them if, as a result of steadily expanding competition, they have to pay more interest on their loans.
Mind you, even with the coming into force of the new small loans bill borrowers will be paying 2 per cent a month on the majority of loans, because the majority of such loans are under $300. The Household Finance Company points out that 68 per cent of all the loans they make are under $300, and the rate of interest will continue to be 2 per cent on all such loans. Of course, it is the people who borrow small amounts who are generally the ones who are so hard pressed.
I think we should keep in mind that the reason the small loans companies are doing such a tremendous business today, and I do not think anybody will dispute that, is partly -I was going to say. largely but I will say partly-as the result of government policy. I believe this session will go down in history as the debtor and creditor session, because we are having more bills to lend money to people than we have ever had before. There have already been six bills introduced to increase loans to people in one form or another. Now we are having bills to increase the capital of small loans companies so they can make more loans.
Therefore I think we are certainly creating a record from the point of view of making it possible for people to go further and further into debt. It looks as though the only way this government can hope to bolster a high economy is to help people go steadily further and further into debt, even if the rate has to be 2 per cent a month.
Some people say that these people must be able to borrow money, and ask if we are going to deprive them of that right. I would say no. But I would suggest that the government has some responsibility in that regard. We have chartered banks in this country. We have 11 of them, with branches in every town. Here in Ottawa it is hard to find a street without running into two or three branches of chartered banks. Surely these banks could handle this business. The Canadian Bank of Commerce has already led the way in showing how it can be done. We amended the Bank Act, at the time of the last revision, in order to allow the chartered banks to take chattel mortgages. Therefore the chartered banks are now in a position in which they can very well make personal loans to the people and thereby relieve the small loans companies of a great deal of work.
I think it would be a good idea if we could cut down the arpount of work or the
Private Bills
amount of business the small loans companies do. In fact I think it would be a good thing if we could put them right out of business and let the people depend upon the chartered banks to do their lending. In order to help the people who are down and out, I think the government could very well bring in certain legislation along the lines, we will say, of the farm improvement loan plan under which they guarantee the banks against the losses. I think we need some kind of policy whereby loans can be guaranteed to small industrial workers so they can get money when they need it without having to pay the exorbitant rate of interest of 2 per cent per month.
For these two reasons, as I say, we intend to support the amendment.

He said: Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank hon. members of this house for agreeing unanimously to the postponement of the other business before the house in order that this resolution may be proceeded with for the time there is left this evening.
In presenting this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer briefly to Hansard of Thursday, July 21, 1955, in which it is recorded that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and I had a little interchange in the house. As reported at page 6528 of Hansard I asked the Minister of Transport the following question:
Has the Department of Transport any plans at present under way for any form of coastguard service on the great lakes or anything resembling it?
The minister replied as follows:
I think I should say that the answer to that question- is no. I have a memorandum on the subject which starts off by saying that the subject was reviewed a number of years ago. At that time I am told that the conclusion that was reached was that it would cost approximately $9 million at that time for the capital expenditures necessary to start a coastguard service and that thereafter the annual cost would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $3 million.
It is with those remarks that I should like to start off. I should like to point out to the minister that this need for a coastguard service on the great lakes has arisen largely since the end of world war II, and that any survey carried out prior to that time would have no application at the present time. Second, the amount of money that was suggested by the minister is, I feel, quite out of line. I believe the cost would be much less. Consequently the first remarks I should like to make are as follows.
I should like to deal first of all with the limitation of the scope of this resolution. In this regard I should say that the resolution contemplates coastguard service on only the lower lakes, namely lake Ontario, lake Erie, lake St. Clair and lake Huron. In addition to that, any such proposed service as that which
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite).]
I have in mind would be limited to the summer months, possibly from the middle of May until the end of September. The third limitation that I have in mind is this. The resolution does not contemplate one aspect of coastguard service, namely the law-enforcement provisions dealing with customs and excise. The resolution is primarily aimed at first of all, search and rescue activities on the great lakes; second, the prevention of accidents on the great lakes; and third, increased navigation aids.
First of all I think we should look at the present facilities available. First I shall deal with search and rescue. As the minister pointed out on a previous occasion as recorded in Hansard of Thursday, July 21, 1955, at page 6528, there are certain other branches of government dealing with coastguard service such as the Royal Canadian Air Force, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and so on. The Royal Canadian Air Force base at Trenton, Ontario, does carry out a search and rescue operation on the great lakes. The Ontario provincial police, under certain conditions, if requested by the municipalities, carry out certain limited beach patrols. The municipalities themselves have lifeguard service on beaches to prevent drowning accidents, or to try to do so, anyway. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police have five patrol boats on the great lakes, at Windsor, Sarnia, Toronto and Kingston. I believe they also have one at Sault Ste. Marie, but that is outside the scope that is contemplated in this resolution.
In addition, the United States coastguard will come in and assist if a request is made by the Canadian government. The Royal Canadian Navy have on the great lakes certain craft which assist in rescue work if necessary. There are also some fine volunteer services. For instance, I understand that under the auspices of the Port Credit yacht club last summer an organization called the lake Ontario search and rescue organization was set up which deals with the area, I believe, from Oshawa to the United States border. It is purely a volunteer service, but I understand it is intended to carry out the necessary service there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the minister possibly was not in his seat when I commenced my remarks and said that I was limiting this resolution to the lower great lakes, namely lake Ontario, lake Huron, lake Erie and lake St. Clair.

As I have pointed out, there are these various services on the lakes at the present time. I understand that they are competent, and so far their activities have been very good. Co-operation by the United States coast guard has been good and has been a help on certain occasions. Then, Mr. Speaker, I suppose the obvious question arises, what is the criticism of these facilities if they are there? Why propose this motion?
Well, first of all, the main objection is that under present conditions on the lakes the present search and rescue facilities are absolutely inadequate. Second, the facilities there completely lack any co-ordination. In this respect I should like to refer to one or two newspaper clippings. I might say that coordination is very important in rescue work, particularly when a life is involved, such as a drowning accident or people being left out on the lake all night. The question of co-ordination and timing is an essential element, and that is what seems to be lacking. I refer to a clipping from the London Free Press, dated July 25, 1955, entitled, "Patrol Service Need Cited Following Search at 'Port' ". The editorial says:
Garnet Speers, local marine man, stated there was much need for co-ordinated safety measures.
This appeared following an accident, and it continues:
Mr. Speers stated this morning that successful lake searches depend on the prompt receipt of reports and as accurate as possible bearings taken from shore. "There is a lot of lake out there'', he explained. Because of the lack of a Canadian coastguard service, the more experienced yachtsmen are alert to the need for fast patrol and search service.
Then I should like to refer very briefly to an editorial in a very large weekly, the Tillsonburg News, dated July 28, 1955. I believe the Tillsonburg News is one of the largest weeklies in the province of Ontario. It reads as follows:
From the large number of small boat accidents on the great lakes and the number of lives lost, and in many cases the delay in organization of adequate search or rescue efforts, it would appear that the present government agencies are far from adequate in providing the necessary help, and that steps are necessary to provide a more closely knit and readily available service.
With due regard for the effectiveness of the R.C.A.F. communication and rescue fleet at Trenton, which Mr. Marler pointed out had the responsibility of co-ordinating the search and rescue activities of not only government ships but also other ships on the great lakes, we suggest that it is not in much of a position to save a boatload of persons swamped off Port Burwell or in Long Point bay.
The third aspect of criticism of the present facilities is that municipalities and provincial
Search and Rescue
authorities can extend their activity only so far into the water because of the international aspect of the great lakes.
The fourth criticism of the present facilities is that there is no co-ordinating service. There is no one to prevent small craft going out in bad weather, and there is no one to regulate the use of these craft. There are some young people who like to run up and down amongst the bathers in speed boats and engage in other smart-aleck activities. Then, too, the present services lack organization. I am thinking of an event that occurred near Sarnia, when some people were reported missing. After a day or so they were located quite safe in a harbour. I understand that the estimated cost of this particular rescue work, if it could be called such, was between $40,000 and $50,000. If there had been some form of co-ordinating coastguard service, these people would have been located a lot sooner. My contention is that there is an absolute necessity at the present time for an increased coastguard service on the great lakes which contemplates the things I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks.
I have here a great many newspaper clippings, but I do not intend to take up the time of the house by reading them. I believe all hon. members who live in southern Ontario are quite aware of the number of drowning and boating accidents that take place on the great lakes during the summertime. I do not think a day goes by when there is not an accident or a drowning, and often there are many in one day. However, I should like to read one or two clippings just to illustrate to hon. members from other parts of the country that this is not something I am pulling out of a hat, so to speak.
I refer to a clipping from the Sentinel-Review of Woodstock, Ontario, dated August 10, 1955. The heading is, "Undertow Draws Seven to Death", and that happened at Wasaga Beach. Then there is another clipping from the Sentinel-Review of Wednesday, September 21, and the heading is, "Three Oxford Centre Men Missing on Lake Erie Fishing Expedition". There is a heading in the Toronto Telegram of August 30, 1955, "Lashed By Storm Fourteen Hours, Two Anglers Saved On Lake". Then there is some editorial comment on this matter, and I refer to the Globe and Mail of Toronto, July 25, 1955. The heading of the editorial is, "Lake Coastguards Needed". This editorial comments on the many unseasoned operators of power boats. It says:
Too many unseasoned operators of power boats do not know that hand-propelled and sailing craft have protective right of way which all powered boats must respect. And many owners of speed

Search and Rescue
boats who do know the rules still make a sport ol giving canoes, skiffs and small sailboats a mighty wash from their wakes.
The lower lakes, including Georgian bay, require patrols, partly to enforce the law, but also to engage in rescue work when accidents beset any water craft. Safety on our waterways is just as important as on our highways.
I could read many more newspaper clippings, but I believe many hon. members will recall the more shocking accidents. I think the summer before last there was an accident in lake Ontario off Oakville in which nine sea scouts were drowned. They went out in a boat, and there was no one to warn them that bad weather was likely to set in within a short time.
It is very difficult to get any figures, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the number of accidents and the number of drownings on the great lakes. I have made efforts to do this, but I have not been successful because apparently no record is kept. I repeat that all hon. members who live in the southern part of Ontario know quite well that all you have to do is pick up the newspaper any day during the summer months or early fall, and you will see the results of the lack of a coastguard service.
Now, why has this need arisen, as it has, largely since the end of world war II? I believe all hon. members know there has been a great increase in the population of southern Ontario, just as there has been an increase in the population in the other parts of the country. The second reason, and I think the main reason, is the great increase in real wages and the increase in leisure time. This increase in leisure time is not confined entirely to city people. Those people who live in rural areas, as a result of the increased use of farm machinery also have a little more time on their hands than they had 50 years ago. As a result, there has been a great increase in boats of all types on the great lakes.
Fortunately I have been able to obtain some figures to illustrate this. As hon. members may know, all motors of 10 horsepower and over have to be registered. There is no fee for this registration. Apparently it is merely a case of registering for record purposes. It is very difficult to draw too many conclusions from the figures, and I am giving them only to show the increase in the number of small boats in the southern part of Ontario.
In 1950 the number of 10 horsepower on our motors in Ontario was 21,220. Five years later, in 1955, the number was 54,145. In 1955 alone the number increased by 15,483. This does not include a great number of boats which are powered by motors of less than 10 horsepower. It does not include rowboats, or anything of that nature. The only

thing these figures can show is the tremendous increase in boating activity on the lower great lakes.	.
I discussed the matter with a number of people who have boats at Long Point bay on lake Erie. Estimates have been made that there are well over 1,000 boats of more than 10 horsepower there alone, and the figure is nearer 1,500. There are a great many, of course, with motors under 10 horsepower. It is very difficult to locate where all the boats are. A 10 horsepower motor can be registered at any customs office, and you also find all sorts of inland places which technically have boats registered there. It is extremely difficult to know at what port and on what lakes they are used.
I think it is apparent, however, that there has been a vast increase in the number of small boats in use today. Not only that, but there has been an increase in activities on the lakes. We have many picnic groups from factories, service clubs and other organizations which go to the great lakes, rent or charter boats and go fishing. Often these boats are very old, and when the motors break down these parties are left out on the lakes. It happens time after time.
While the owners and operators of commercial launches and fishing boats are no doubt quite experienced people, the ordinary small boat owner is very inexperienced at navigation. They frequently go out on the lakes and a storm comes up. They get lost or swamped and they really do not know what to do. This is the cause of many accidents. In this regard I would point out that many small boat owners who wish to take their boats out from ports on lakes Erie and Huron find there is no place where they can get proper information regarding the impending weather. Believe me, this is extremely necessary on the lower great lakes, because the local weather picture can change in an hour or so; it can change just as quickly as that. I would also point out that there is no one at any of these ports or places where boats are located to prevent boats going out, or to regulate traffic.
At the present time there is a rescue service, as I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks. This is composed of a combination of the R.C.M.P., the R.C.A.F. and others; but it seems to me that the search and rescue service, as it is called, does only one thing. It searches for dead bodies after people have been drowned, and I think we require a much more useful service, Mr. Speaker.
I have a few suggestions to make concerning the type of coastguard service I hope the

minister will consider. I might also point out that I do not think it will cost too much money because like other hon. members, and particularly the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) who is always talking about economy, I do not believe in wasting money or throwing it around where it is not necessary.
I am not suggesting that we have an elaborate coastguard service such as they have in the United States. I do not believe it is warranted under the circumstances, and I think it would be difficult to maintain. I agree with the minister in that respect.
The first thing I would like to suggest is how we might go about financing a service such as I envisage without having it cost too much money. All the boats with motors of 10 horsepower or more which operate on the great lakes at the present time are required to get a licence. It is a strange thing to observe that the owners can be fined $100 for not having a licence, but the licence does not actually cost anything. That seems rather peculiar to me. It is like something out of Alice in Wonderland.
I suggest that the people who have boats on the great lakes would not object to paying a small licence fee of $5 or $10, depending on the horsepower of the motor, if they were to have a coastguard service of some kind, a rescue service and navigation aids, and so on. I have spoken to many people who have boats, and all of them have said they would be delighted to pay a small fee if they could obtain some kind of service. This would not defray the entire cost of operating such a service, but it would go a long way toward defraying the cost of a coastguard service. It is only fair that the people who own boats should not bear the whole cost of a coastguard service, because many people who would benefit do not own boats but go to the lakes to fish, swim, or go on excursions on holidays or week ends, and the general public should pay something toward the cost.
The third suggestion I would make is that coastguard officers be placed at appropriate spots along the shores of lakes Ontario, Erie, Huron and St. Clair. As I pointed out this job would be seasonal, from the middle of May to end of September. These officers could be university students. This would provide helpful employment for students who are looking for summer work. Many university students have to take work at very small wages during the summer at summer hotels and elsewhere, and usually they must work indoors. This service would provide healthful outdoor work for university students and would fit right into their program from the point of view of time.
Search and Rescue
If appointed, these officers could perform the following duties. They could be provided with meteorological reports which they could post every day. They could give the necessary information regarding weather forecasts for the succeeding 12 or 24 hours. They could post these notices on piers and beaches and in places where there are boats. Storm warnings could be given by these officers in order to warn people not to go out on the water. They could use the black cones which are usually used along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
I would also suggest that the coastguard officers should be trained in life saving and artificial respiration. The new Swedish method developed by Colonel Nealson, a Swedish gentleman, which has recently come into vogue, could be taught to them. They should be provided with life-saving devices, oxygen, artificial respiration aids, and a first, aid course.
They should have the power to prohibit boats going out if a storm is pending, and they should also be empowered to regulate traffic. The United States coastguard has this authority. If an officer is aware that a storm might blow up in an hour or so he could prohibit boats going out, and suitable penalties could be levied if his warning were disregarded. The officer could also control smart alecks in boats who try to swamp other boats just to give them a thrill. I am sure that any hon. member who has been on the lakes in the summertime has seen people doing this dangerous thing. The main work of these coastguard officers, if I might suggest a name for them, would be to coordinate rescue services and activities. The main trouble at the present time is that there is not sufficient co-ordination among the various forms of rescue work presently on the lakes.
I would like at this point to refer to some remarks made by the Minister of Transport. In reply to a question I asked on June 21, 1955, the minister said, as reported at page 6528 of Hansard, and I shall quote directly from Hansard:
But how does the information get to the R.C.A.F. and under whose authority do they go to these cases?

I think it is because somebody
communicates with them in some way or other, by radio, by telephone, by telegram or something.
To my mind that is the greatest argument for having some co-ordinated service. If coastguard officers were located at appropriate places along the shore to do nothing else for a few months in the summer but be there and have it known to the local authorities that they were there, if they issued certain instructions as to whom to get in

touch with they would be performing a valuable service. The time element is most important when people are upset in the water or lost out on the lake, and this business of calling the R.C.A.F. in Trenton the next day to go out and help find the bodies is not of much help to the relatives of those who have been drowned.

speechtext:
I have travelled along a considerable portion of the shores of the great lakes, but I am not familiar with every single mile. All the resolution asks the government to do is take into consideration the advisability of bringing down legislation. I am sure there are plenty of people in the Department of Transport who could take two or three days off and figure this out. I have not had the opportunity of travelling up and down and around the lakes.
The next thing I should like to deal with is the type of service that might be provided. If we are going to have coastguard officers along the coast to act as co-ordinators it might be advisable to have boats available to do rescue work if necessary. These officers would co-ordinate the work of the R.C.A.F., the R.C.M.P. and the provincial police, but I think where necessary-this decision would have to be made by the Department of Transport- there should be duty boats which could go out if necessary.
These duty boats could be located where there were the greatest concentrations of small craft during the summer. I am not suggesting for one minute that the department should buy a number of yachts or patrol boats, but I am suggesting that the department might hire boats to be used as duty boats in places such as Toronto, Oakville and Hamilton on lake Ontario, and Port Colborne, Port Dover, Port Stanley, Port Burwell on lake Erie, and so on.
It might be possible to hire fishing boats during the summer months when the catches are not so large. Many fishermen would be glad to have jobs operating duty boats. Fishing boats would be the best because their crews would be highly experienced, many of them are equipped with ship to shore radio, and are quite speedy. Then there are many persons owning large launches and I am sure these could be obtained on a contract basis to be operated as duty boats. It should not cost too much money.
iMr. Nesbitt.]
In certain congested areas such as the Toronto area and possibly the Long Point area it might be necessary to have a constant patrol during the summer months. Again this is something the department would have to decide. I merely throw it out as a suggestion that it might be advisable to cover the congested areas where people are running around upsetting small boats and that kind of thing.
There is another important thing to be considered. I think the department should lay down rules requiring all small boats to be equipped with flares or smoke bombs, and also with life jackets. It would be up to the local officers to see that these rules were enforced. In other words, no boat would be permitted to go out on the lakes without a certain number of life preservers and flares or smoke bombs. If they happened to get into trouble they could send up signals.
I would like to make my remarks a bit longer, but because of the shortness of time and because other hon. members would like to speak, I shall not elaborate further. Both the minister and his parliamentary assistant come from a province which is not associated in any way with the great lakes, and they may not have the same sympathy as those who come from southern Ontario and who are more immediately concerned with this matter. I feel that all hon. members, who come from southern Ontario, regardless of party, should support this resolution. I know perfectly well that it will not get to a vote tonight, but whether or not they support it in the house they should support it privately. It is merely a question of having the Department of Transport look into the advisability of bringing down legislation in this regard. This evening I have simply passed out a few suggestions as to what I consider would be necessary, and even these would probably require some modification.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF COASTGUARD SERVICE ON GREAT LAKES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Northumberland county which I have the honour to represent lies on the north shore of lake Ontario and for that reason I have a particular interest in the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Oxford, which is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide for the establishment of a coastguard service on the great lakes of Canada.
At first glance this appeared to me to be a worthy objective, but tonight when I heard the hon. member put his reservations on the record I realized that he had cut his own resolution to pieces and it had therefore lost much of its effectiveness. The hon. member's first reservation was that he would confine

this to the lower great lakes and to the summer months. Then there is to be nothing in the way of law enforcement or customs collections. When I read this resolution on the order paper I thought the hon. member had in mind patterning the Canadian coastguard service on that of the United States.
We all know that the United States coastguard service has an enviable reputation and is noted for its efficiency and on many occasions for its heroism. We do not have a unified service in Canada, but the various agencies of government are organized to perform much the same duties as those performed by the United States coastguard. It is my submission that what is being done in Canada does not suffer from comparison with what is being done by the United States coastguard service.
The agencies of government which are concerned in Canada are mainly the Department of National Defence, the Department of Transport and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The hon. member has referred to the lack of co-ordination in the Canadian system, but I submit that there is considerable evidence of co-ordination in our system. I should like to refer to what the Royal Canadian Air Force is doing in this regard, and I quote from an air force release No. 8620 dealing with search and rescue in Canada, as follows:
From British Columbia to Newfoundland, from the 49th parallel to Canada's Arctic archipelago, men and women of the R.C.A.F.'s search and rescue organization stand ready to answer the call of distress.
And again:
The R.C.A.F. is charged with the co-ordination and supervision of all search and rescue activity in Canada, and with the provision of all primary search and rescue facilities. This includes responsibility for search and rescue operations involving aircraft in distress, marine distress cases on the east and west coasts of Canada and portions of the great lakes, and, as a secondary role, provision of aid in any necessary circumstances. . . .
Control is carried out from six major co-ordination centres at Torbay, Newfoundland, Halifax, Trenton (Ont.), Winnipeg, Edmonton and Vancouver. Aircraft earmarked for mercy flights or search operations are stationed at Torbay, Newfoundland; Greenwood, N.S.; Goose Bay, Labrador; Trenton; Winnipeg; Churchill, Man.; Edmonton; Whitehorse, Y.T., and Vancouver, and although planes at these points held for specific search and rescue work are allowed to carry out other duties, they are never allowed to undertake jobs which would prevent them from being instantly ready for their primary responsibility.
The list of primary facilities of the air force for search and rescue work also includes helicopters, and a group of specially trained airmen who have been given an intensive course in para-rescue work near Jasper, Alberta.

speechtext:
I continue to quote, Mr. Speaker:
Nerve centres of the work are the major rescue co-ordination centres, for from them are directed all operations by search and rescue. Ready for instant use are lists of all service facilities ready to be called upon, including navy carrier planes in addition to R.C.A.F. aircraft, bodies of men for search parties, and vessels, as well as outstanding civilian facilities, such as charter companies, tugboats and the like.
At Trenton, Ontario, which is very close to my own county of Northumberland, there is the No. 102 communications and rescue flight. This unit is responsible for the co-ordination of all search and rescue work on the great lakes and for moving not only government ships but privately owned ships in case of accidents. I know that the services of helicopters are being used more and more in the search and rescue work, and I believe that the Department of Transport has under consideration the further use of helicopters in this connection.
The Royal Canadian Navy is also playing an important part in search and rescue work. It has numerous escort and patrol ships which can perform the same type of service. The Department of Transport itself carries out very important functions, such as putting down aids to navigation, marking channels, carrying supplies, icebreaking, and also furnishing very valuable weather forecasts from seven departmental stations. These weather forecasts are given three or four times each day.
The R.C.M.P. also operates patrol boats on the great lakes. I know that on lake Ontario there are two patrol boats operating. The first of these is stationed at Kingston, the Cutknife II. In Toronto another patrol boat is also operating. These R.C.M.P. patrol boats perform a number of coastguard services such as assisting ships in distress, investigating drownings, patrolling the waters when regattas are being held, assisting other police forces, including the United States coastguard service, and performing a check of pleasure boats on behalf of the customs' department. It is therefore evident that we have an effective service already in existence in this country.
The hon. member talked a great deal about providing some protection for small pleasure boats on the great lakes. He evidently has in mind a method of policing small boats operated by tourists in the many resorts on the great lakes, but I think he will agree

Search and Rescue
that the number of resorts where there is a concentration of tourist boats is so large that the government could not hope to provide boats at each of these places. I think it is also obvious that if we had a coastguard service on the great lakes, it would only be by the merest chance that one of these boats would be in a position to render assistance in the case of sudden upset or other dangers in which owners of small pleasure craft might find themselves.
I do not believe that by the methods he has suggested we could deal effectively with the small boat problem, which is the most frequent source of marine accidents. The United States still has many such accidents, although it has a very efficient coastguard service. The hon. member presented no statistics to prove that we have more such accidents than the United States. I think this house should have such evidence before making any decision on this matter.
In my opinion we can better deal with this situation by the following methods. The first is the education of the small boat owners. We should teach them safety measures. I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to a publication produced by the Department of Transport entitled, "Safety Afloat for Owners of Small Boats". This is a very fine publication dealing with the prevention of accidents in the small boat field in this country. On the first page of this publication I find the following:
The great majority of these accidents can be prevented.
This booklet has been prepared with that purpose in mind, to help spread the information that can drastically cut the needless toll in property damage and human suffering, and make for safety afloat for yourself, your family and others.
As I go through this publication I find that there is information regarding life-saving equipment, methods of fire prevention, and also information as to the dangers of overloading these small craft. There is also a very interesting section dealing with the rules of the road, and this gives very important information as to what the owners of these boats should do and what they should not do. I believe if the owners of small boats in Canada would read and follow the advice given in this publication, a great many of these accidents could be avoided.
A second method would be the regulation of the small boat operators themselves, and we do this through a licensing system. I find that, by law, boats fitted temporarily or permanently with motors of 10 horsepower or more are required to be licensed. Such licenses are obtainable free of charge from all customs officers in Canada, and the R.C.M.P. enforces the small vessel licensing regulations. Through a system of licensing

and inspection we are able to make sure that the boats themselves are in a good state of repair.
A third method, I think, to prevent the loss of life would be by seeking the co-operation of local organizations, who would play their part in seeing that proper safety precautions were taken. I think the various tourist associations and the yacht clubs at various points on the great lakes could make a splendid contribution in this regard.
I would also draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the work done by the committee set up by the government in 1949 under the chairmanship of Mr. Justice Clyne, who at that time was chairman of the Canadian maritime commission. The committee was set up by the government to, first, review the existing arrangements for search and rescue work in Canada and, second, make recommendations for improved and more efficient service. The committee reported that while on occasion valuable assistance had been rendered by the United States coastguard service to Canadian ships in Canadian waters, there was no evidence that a large number of casualties in Canadian waters had been prevented by the United States coastguard. Further, it was pointed out that United States ships had been assisted on many occasions by our own Canadian ships.
The committee reported that valuable work had been carried out by the R.C.A.F. search and rescue co-ordinating centres, and praised the work of those centres in detail. The committee recommended that co-ordinating centres be kept informed of the position and movement of all ships, and should be informed of any casualties. It also recommended that we should take the necessary action to ensure safety of life and, if possible, the prevention of damage or loss of any ship and its cargo. There was no recommendation by the committee for the establishment of a coastguard.
The report on marine casualties in the period between April 1946, and 1949 found that in the great majority of these accidents satisfactory assistance had been rendered by government-owned ships, by subsidized companies and by privately-owned ships in the vicinity. In those cases where loss of life had occurred it appeared that the majority of such losses could hardly have been avoided no matter how elaborate a system of search and rescue might have been available on the great lakes at that time.
At the outset of his speech the hon. member for Oxford referred to the cost of such an operation. He quoted the words of the minister in the debate last session to the effect that the establishment of a proper coastguard

2S31
system would cost some $9 million to $12 million, and the maintenance of such a system would cost $3 million per year. This is a large sum of money; and while the hon. member did say that we should confine our efforts to the great lakes I submit that if we are going to set up a proper coastguard system it should extend to all the great lakes and to both the east and west coasts.
While the spending of this amount of money might seem to be justified to some, nevertheless I can think of other dangerous situations in this country where people are regularly losing their lives. If we have any such amount of money to spend I believe we could very well spend it on increasing the railway grade crossing fund, and thus eliminate many of the very dangerous crossings in this country.
I suggest it is not practical to organize a coastguard system on a national basis as outlined by the hon. member for Oxford tonight. The administrative costs would be far too high and out of all proportion to the service obtained. I believe such a system could be organized on a local basis, and I think the responsibility for so organizing rests on the local people in each community. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, to the best of my knowledge there has been no request from the commercial shipping interests that such a coastguard service should be established. I think that is very strong evidence that the need for such an organization has not been fully proven by the hon. member for Oxford.
I indicated at the beginning of my remarks that I come from a riding located on lake Ontario. I can honestly say that I have had no suggestions from individuals, organizations or public bodies that a need for a coastguard service exists at the present time. If the need is not apparent in the area in which I live I cannot believe that it is as great as outlined by the hon. member for Oxford in other areas on the great lakes.
There is also the fact that a very large percentage of these accidents take place on the smaller inland lakes of Ontario. Surely the hon. member would not suggest that the federal government should set up an organization on these inland lakes. Finally, I would say that the functions which would be carried out by such a coastguard organization are now carried out efficiently and satisfactorily, and that the expense of setting up such an organization as that envisaged by the hon. member for Oxford would not be warranted or justified at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to join briefly in the discussion of the resolution introduced by

the hon. member for Oxford proposing the establishment of a coastguard service on the great lakes, I want to say at the outset that I find myself very much in sympathy with the objective he has in mind. Some hon. members may recall that during the debate on the speech from the throne earlier this session I had occasion to refer to this subject matter as it affects the coastal areas of British Columbia. My remarks were made on Friday, January 13, and can be found at page 108 of Hansard. Inasmuch as I used my 40 minutes on that occasion in discussing the subject, I do not intend to repeat now the arguments I used then.
In view of the fact that I come from a constituency in the coastal area of British Columbia I am sure the hon. member for Oxford will appreciate that my interest in this subject extends somewhat beyond the immediate scope of his resolution, and perhaps he may not be surprised if I propose before I take my seat that the resolution should be broadened somewhat. Of course I am not in a position to analyse in any detail the pros and cons of the discussion that took place between the hon. member for Oxford and the hon. member for Northumberland, but I must say that as I listened to the communique, shall I say, that the hon. member for Northumberland read-

It was very close to some of the descriptions I have heard of the functioning of the search and rescue emit and its coordinated service as applied to the Pacific coast of British Columbia. If my own analysis and comparison of the effectiveness of what we have in British Columbia is paralleled by the situation on the great lakes, then I can say that I think the hon. member for Oxford has real grounds for bringing forward this resolution respecting the area which is his particular concern. While, as I stated when I spoke earlier, I recognize some of the value of the search and rescue set-up under the R.C.A.F., I also recognize there is a great deal to be desired before we can have what I consider to be a proper marine rescue service in this country.
I was interested to note the reference made by the hon. member for Northumberland to that publication of the Department of Transport entitled "Safety Afloat". Even assuming that the government is not convinced at once of the advisability of taking certain action, I think perhaps one of the immediate values

Search and Rescue
of this discussion is that it may serve to draw to the attention of a larger number of Canadians the unnecessary hazards to which they subject themselves when they go afloat. I have looked over that particular publication and I must say that I agree with the hon. member for Northumberland about it. I can only wish that it were receiving much more widespread attention than it has hitherto received and that the government, apart from any other consideration, were taking greater pains to ensure that all of those who are concerned were aware of it and were aware of the dangers to which attention is drawn. I certainly agree that much can be accomplished in reducing the hazards of sailing, either on the great lakes or on the sea coasts, by the proper type of educational program in this connection.
I must say that I was pleased to note last autumn that some modest step is being taken to draw to the attention of people the dangers of travelling by boat and that, among other things, steps are being taken to bring up to date the enforcement of the safety regulations with regard to the larger boats which come under licence classifications.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, if this matter is going to receive from the government consideration along the lines I argued earlier this session and along the lines that were argued by the hon. member for Oxford, I feel that anything that is done should be on a national basis. I hardly think we can expect our federal government to take under consideration a plan which is not drawn up along those lines. I should therefore like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron):
That the resolution be amended by inserting therein immediately after the words "great lakes" the words "and coastal waters".
I feel that this amendment does not in any way detract from the argument which has been presented to the house by the hon. member for Oxford, and in which he outlined the needs of his particular area. However, I feel that it may serve to bring into focus this problem of improved marine rescue service as a national problem which affects the people on the great lakes, the people on the coast of British Columbia and undoubtedly the people on the coasts of the Atlantic provinces of Canada.
This is a matter on which I have been frank to say that some things have been done, but to my mind not enough has yet been done. While the vote that is brought down by the Minister of National Defence in this connection for the work done under the R.C.A.F. is all well and good, it still does not bring the problem of marine rescue down to

the level of the waves. I feel that the hon. member for Oxford had a legitimate argument when he said it did not create the kind of closely co-ordinated service which the people generally were aware of, and of which they knew how to take immediate advantage under the emergency situations that from time to time arise as far as our sea coasts or our great inland water areas are concerned.

At this late hour, Mr. Speaker, I shall cut down my remarks considerably. In taking part in this debate on the resolution moved by the hon. member for Oxford I should like to say that I believe he deserves a great deal of credit for bringing this matter to the attention of the government. After the experience he had in the navy during the last war I am sure he is quite competent to advance, as he has done, a great number of reasons why this coastguard service is a worthy project.
I should like to say that I am interested in this matter because the district from which I come has approximately 300 miles of shoreline. That shoreline is all on blue water. It is extremely attractive to summer tourists. It is gradually being filled up with summer visitors from outside. As you know, many of these visitors have their yachts with them, as well as their power boats. Many of the people who live in Bruce have their boats. In addition we have great numbers of fishing vessels which are out a great part of the year. As well, a number of United States

yachts come over to visit us. I am sure these summer visitors are all welcome, and I think they enjoy themselves.
I should like to say that there is a crying need for some kind of co-ordination that has been spoken about by the hon. member for Oxford. I should also like to say that the number of these boats on lake Huron and Georgian bay is increasing each year. As the deep waterway is opened up there will be a greater need for such a coastguard service.
I would make one suggestion, and it is this. If the government see fit to inaugurate something along the lines spoken of by the hon. member for Oxford, during the peak of the summer season when the schools are closed I should hope they might see fit to train some of our sea cadets on some of those
Search and Rescue
boats they will be using. It would be good training for all those boys who have the navy in view for their future life.
I should like to say that the remarks made by the hon. member for Northumberland indicated a defeatist attitude. He did not review any of the arguments made by the hon. member for Oxford, and I am sure he had a great deal of help in preparing that speech which he read off. If the government sees fit in future to take advice from the hon. member for Oxford, I hope that we in Bruce county will get some of the service that is coming to us. We have paid a great deal for service in other parts of the country, and have received none.
